L01 · Introduction to Pharmacology — Session 1 — study guide
**Pharmacology:** the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
**Drug (medication):** any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
**Pharmacologic effect:** a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
**Therapeutic effect:** the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
**Adverse drug reaction (ADR):** an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
**Toxicity:** harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
**Chemical name:** describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
**Generic name:** the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
**Brand (trade) name:** the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
**Prodrug:** an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
**Poisons** are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.
Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug — ADME.
Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
Pharmacogenomics = how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
This map covers the whole lecture: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.
Drugs bind receptors by **covalent** bonds (strong, often irreversible), **electrostatic** bonds (most common) or **hydrophobic** bonds (weak).
**Chirality:** over half of drugs are mirror-image pairs (enantiomers); one is usually much more potent, yet most are sold as 50:50 mixtures.
**PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name — it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.**
Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.
Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
If a patient says they take "Tylenol" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.
Precise vocabulary (generic names, therapeutic vs. adverse effects) protects patients.
More than half of prescriptions in the USA are for generic drugs.
Weak bonds need a precise fit, so they are **more selective**. Aspirin’s covalent bond to platelet cyclooxygenase lasts until new platelets are made.
Acetaminophen (generic) is sold as Tylenol and under many store brands.

t: Why prescribe by generic name? One drug has ONE generic name but can hide under SEVERAL brand names — so brand-name products can conceal duplicate therapy and cause double-dosing.
Pharmaco**K**inetics = the body **K**eeps the drug moving (ADME). Pharmaco**D**ynamics = what the **D**rug **D**oes to the body.
ADR = **A**t normal **D**oses, **R**eaction is harmful. Toxicity = **T**oo much (exceeds the therapeutic range).
**Efficacy:** how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
**Effectiveness:** how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
Drug interactions can also reduce real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy.
**Benefit vs. risk:** the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
**Adverse-event reporting:** ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
**Double-blind:** neither subjects nor evaluators know who gets drug or placebo. **Crossover:** each subject gets every treatment in turn.
**IRB:** the committee at each trial site that approves the ethics of the study; participants give informed consent.
Where new drugs come from — Natural products: plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.
Synthetic & biotech: designed small molecules; recombinant proteins.
Biologics: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
Drug repurposing: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
From discovery to patient: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline — approval is the exception, not the rule.
Phase I: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
Phase II: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
Phase III: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
Phase IV: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
Every approved drug has passed through a structured development and regulatory pipeline (Phases I–IV).
Phase II has the **highest failure rate** — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
Phase III usually enrolls **thousands** of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
Less than one-third of drugs studied in humans survive clinical trials and reach the market.
To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has **no fixed duration**.
Marketing requires a **New Drug Application (NDA)** after Phase III; human testing starts only after an **IND** (Investigational New Drug) application.
Strength of evidence: case reports < cohort and case-control studies < **randomized controlled trials** (the gold standard: randomization balances confounders).
Postmarketing surveillance (Phase IV) is where rare adverse effects are often first detected — trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. **Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?**

**Clinical pearl:** risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.
A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an **abbreviated new drug application (ANDA)** that requires bioequivalence data.
Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects — the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
Adverse events that are both **serious and unexpected** must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.
Dietary supplements are regulated as food under DSHEA (1994), so they get no full FDA drug review.
FDA MedWatch — an adverse-event reporting system.

t: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
Phase III — not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
Phase III is what most people picture as "the" clinical trial, but regulatory decisions already begin shaping the drug long before that.

Phase: Phase II · Primary purpose: Preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile · Typical population: A few hundred patients with the target condition · How to tell apart: First look at whether it works

Phase: Phase III · Primary purpose: Confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale · Typical population: Hundreds to thousands, often multi-site · How to tell apart: Largest **pre-approval** trial
Phase: Phase IV · Primary purpose: Postmarketing surveillance after approval · Typical population: The general prescribed population · How to tell apart: **After approval**; catches rare effects

What changes it · Efficacy: Not covered in materials · Effectiveness: Real-world adherence, comorbidities (and drug interactions — SG)

t: Phase I population: slides say Phase I: a small group of healthy volunteers. Textbook says Phase I: 20–100 healthy volunteers — but if significant toxicity is expected (cancer, AIDS therapy), volunteer **patients with the disease** are used instead.
Phase II size: slides say Phase II: a few hundred patients with the target condition. Textbook says Phase II: a modest number of patients (100–200) with the target disease.
Why are rare adverse effects found after approval? Trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events — so they show up in Phase IV, in the general prescribed population.
Phases by question: **I** = Is it safe (healthy volunteers)? **II** = Is there an effect? **III** = Is it confirmed at scale? **IV** = Is it still safe in everyone?
Effica**C**y = **C**ontrolled conditions. Effecti**V**eness = real-world **V**ariables (adherence, comorbidities).
**Drug target:** the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
**Receptor:** a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
**Signal transduction:** the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
**Pharmacologic response:** the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
Full agonist — maximal receptor activation.
Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity.
Competitive antagonist — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
Noncompetitive antagonist — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
Irreversible antagonist — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.
**Kd:** the drug concentration that fills half the receptors; a low Kd means high affinity.
The pathway: drug → target → signal transduction → response. Every pharmacodynamics topic for the rest of the course maps onto this chain.
Receptor concept: Drug + Receptor → Drug-Receptor Complex → Cellular Response.
This single chain underlies agonism, antagonism, potency, and efficacy — all describe different features of this interaction.
Five major drug target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.
Ion channels: directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.
Enzymes: drugs can inhibit or, less commonly, activate an enzyme's activity.
Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.
Most drugs target receptors or enzymes — ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.
An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal; a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
**Spare receptors:** a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
**Irreversible antagonist** effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is **not** due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
**Allosteric modulators** bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).
Agonist-induced **desensitization** (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.
Targets beyond receptors: **enzymes** (statins on HMG-CoA reductase), **transporters** (digitalis on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; antidepressants) and **structural proteins** (colchicine on tubulin).
Five signaling mechanisms carry a drug’s message into the cell: intracellular receptor, receptor tyrosine kinase, cytokine receptor (JAK-STAT), ion channel and G protein (compared in the table).
Albuterol is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.
Binding activates the β2 receptor → increases intracellular cAMP.
Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
**This is the same receptor-to-response logic you will reuse for every agonist drug this term.**
Albuterol bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.
Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
Propranolol markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.
Glucocorticoids will not stop an acute asthma attack within minutes: gene-acting drugs need hours to make new proteins.
Phosphodiesterase inhibitors prolong second messengers: milrinone (cAMP) and sildenafil (cGMP).
Albuterol — selective β2-adrenergic agonist (example of agonism).

t: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
Study-guide distractor: "has no effect on receptor activity whatsoever" matches none of the agonist/antagonist types.
Type: Full agonist · What it does at the receptor: Maximal receptor activation · Dose-response curve: Not covered in materials · How to tell apart: Reaches maximal activation
Type: Partial agonist · What it does at the receptor: Submaximal activation · Dose-response curve: Not covered in materials · How to tell apart: Submaximal **even at full occupancy**

Type: Inverse agonist · What it does at the receptor: Reduces baseline (constitutive) activity · Dose-response curve: Not covered in materials · How to tell apart: Lowers activity **below normal with no agonist present**

Type: Competitive antagonist · What it does at the receptor: Reversibly competes at the same site · Dose-response curve: **Shifts right, same Emax** · How to tell apart: Overcome by more agonist (surmountable)
Type: Noncompetitive antagonist · What it does at the receptor: Binds elsewhere or irreversibly · Dose-response curve: **Lowers Emax** · How to tell apart: Plateaus lower instead of shifting right
Type: Irreversible antagonist · What it does at the receptor: Permanently inactivates the receptor · Dose-response curve: **Lowers Emax** · How to tell apart: Lasts until new receptor is synthesized
Target: Receptors · What it is / does: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear · Note: Most common target (with enzymes)

t: Why can more agonist overcome a competitive antagonist? Both compete **reversibly for the same site** — flood the site with agonist and it wins, so the curve shifts right but the same Emax is still reached.
Why does albuterol open the airways? β2 activation → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.
**C**ompetitive = **C**an be outcompeted (shift right). **N**oncompetitive = **N**o full ceiling (lower Emax).
**Potency:** how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
**Efficacy (Emax):** the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
**EC₅₀:** the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
**Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).**
**Quantal dose-response:** ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
**Therapeutic window:** the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.
The sigmoidal dose-response curve: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
EC₅₀ is read off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax.
Lower EC₅₀ = more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); curves reaching the same plateau height have identical Emax (efficacy).
A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.
A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers is the therapeutic index itself.
Dose-response curves describe potency and efficacy.
Potency clinically matters for dosing — not for choosing the "better" drug.
Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
With a narrow TI, a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic — which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
Students should be able to name all four narrow-TI drugs without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.
No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are **selective**, not specific.
Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.
**Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.**

t: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.
Definition · Potency: How much drug is needed to get an effect · Efficacy (Emax): The maximum effect the drug can produce
Measured by · Potency: EC₅₀ — **lower EC₅₀ = more potent** · Efficacy (Emax): Plateau height — **higher Emax = more efficacious**
On the curve · Potency: Curve farther **left** · Efficacy (Emax): Curve plateaus **higher**
Clinical weight · Potency: Matters for **dosing**, not for picking the "better" drug · Efficacy (Emax): Matters **much more** — potent + low efficacy may be useless
ED₅₀ vs. TD₅₀ · Wide TI: Far apart — large safety margin · Narrow TI: Close together — small safety margin

t: Why do narrow-TI drugs need blood levels? The effective dose and the toxic dose sit so close together that a small dosing error can push the patient from effective to toxic.
Why does efficacy beat potency clinically? Potency only changes the dose you give; efficacy sets the ceiling of what the drug can achieve at any dose.
Narrow-TI drugs — "**W**atch **L**evels **D**uring **P**rescribing": **W**arfarin, **L**ithium, **D**igoxin, **P**henytoin.
TI = **T**oxic over **E**ffective → TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic on top).
A — Absorption: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
D — Distribution: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
M — Metabolism: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
E — Excretion: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
**Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.**
First-pass effect: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.
**Volume of distribution (Vd):** a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
**pKa:** the pH at which a drug is half ionized and half nonionized.
ADME is the organizing skeleton for the rest of the lecture — each remaining pharmacokinetics section is one ADME letter in depth.
ADME determines how much drug reaches its target and for how long.
Metabolism (M arrow → liver) and Excretion (E arrow → kidney) are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug; Absorption and Distribution govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
First-pass route: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.
**Plasma protein binding:** only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
**Lipid solubility:** lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
**Tissue perfusion:** highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space.
Blood-brain barrier — **Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot?** Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.
Efflux transporters (like P-glycoprotein) can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.
First-pass loss can happen in the **gut wall** (e.g., intestinal CYP3A4) as well as the liver; grapefruit juice inhibits gut-wall metabolism and P-glycoprotein, raising absorption of some drugs.
**P-glycoprotein (MDR1)** pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.
**Ion trapping:** weak acids are excreted faster in **alkaline** urine; weak bases faster in **acidic** urine.
Drugs cross membranes by **lipid diffusion** (the main route), aqueous pores, **carriers** (saturable) or endocytosis (vitamin B₁₂, iron).
Only the **nonionized** form crosses lipid membranes: a weak acid is mostly nonionized when pH < pKa, a weak base when pH > pKa (Henderson-Hasselbalch).
Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism; oral dosing passes through the liver first.
Because the liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug first, some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.
A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.
Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.

t: Why is IV bioavailability 100%? The whole dose enters the bloodstream directly — there is no absorption step and no trip through the liver first.
Why does sublingual skip first-pass? It drains into systemic veins, not the portal vein — so the drug reaches the body before the liver can inactivate it.

Pharmacology studies how drugs interact with living systems: **pharmacokinetics** is what the body does to the drug (ADME), and **pharmacodynamics** is what the drug does to the body.
Learn and prescribe by **generic name** — brand names can hide a shared ingredient and cause unintentional double-dosing.
Drugs move from discovery through preclinical testing, **Phase I–III** trials, FDA review, and **Phase IV** postmarketing surveillance — where rare adverse effects are often first found.
Drugs act on five target classes; a **competitive antagonist** shifts the dose-response curve right (same Emax), while a **noncompetitive/irreversible** antagonist lowers Emax.

**Potency** (EC₅₀) is the dose needed and **efficacy** (Emax) is the ceiling — efficacy matters more — and narrow-TI drugs (**warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin**) need careful dosing and blood levels.
Oral drugs face **first-pass** hepatic metabolism that lowers bioavailability (IV = 100%), and distribution depends on protein binding, lipid solubility, perfusion, and barriers like the BBB.
L02 · Introduction to Pharmacology — Session 2 — study guide
Drug metabolism = how the body chemically transforms drugs.
Phase I — Functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis.
Phase II — Conjugation: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation.
**Enzyme inhibition:** a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.
**Enzyme induction:** a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.
**Cytochrome P450** (in the liver’s smooth endoplasmic reticulum) does most Phase I work and has low substrate specificity: lipid-soluble drugs are its common thread.
Why metabolize? To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete.
To activate a prodrug into its active form.
To produce an active metabolite that contributes to (or extends) the drug effect.
**Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite — the basis of some drug-induced organ injury.**
Phase I is primarily carried out by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group.
Phase II attaches a polar group to the molecule, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.
Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.
Inhibition slows clearance (substrate level rises); induction speeds clearance (substrate level falls).

Acetaminophen is mostly conjugated (glucuronide/sulfate); in overdose glutathione is depleted and the toxic metabolite (NAPQI) injures the liver — **N-acetylcysteine** given within 8–16 hours protects against fulminant hepatotoxicity.
Share of liver P450: CYP3A4 about 30%, CYP2C9 about 20%, CYP1A2 about 15%, CYP2D6 about 5%.
**Commensal gut microbiota** (gut bacteria) metabolize drugs too: they inactivate digoxin, so antibiotics such as erythromycin can double digoxin levels.
An inducer can speed up its own metabolism (**pharmacokinetic tolerance**): the same dose works less over time.
CYP450 interactions are one of the highest-yield concepts in all of pharmacology — nearly every major drug class has at least one clinically important CYP interaction.
**Example: Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises.**
Inhibition pushes a substrate's level ABOVE 100% of baseline (toxicity risk); induction pushes it BELOW 100% (therapeutic-failure risk).
Inhibiting the CYP that clears a substrate is especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.
Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.
Liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis) slows metabolism enough that ordinary doses can cause coma. CYP3A4 handles over 50% of liver-metabolized prescriptions.
**Diet and environment:** smoking, charcoal-broiled food and cruciferous vegetables induce CYP1A; grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A.
Stopping an inducer is as risky as starting one: when the inducer stops, warfarin metabolism slows, levels rise and bleeding can follow.
NAPQI (from acetaminophen) is the textbook example of a toxic metabolite produced by normal Phase I metabolism — previewing the acetaminophen toxicity lecture.

**IN**hibitor = level goes **IN**to the danger zone (↑, toxicity). In**DU**cer = level goes **D**own (↓, failure).
Phase **I** = **I**nitial change (oxidize, reduce, hydrolyze — CYP450). Phase **II** = **T**ag it (conjugate a polar group → water-soluble).
Drug excretion = clearing drug from the body.
**Glomerular filtration:** free (unbound) drug passes from blood into the renal tubule based on molecular size.
**Tubular secretion:** active transporters move additional drug from blood into the tubule.
**Tubular reabsorption:** lipophilic, un-ionized drug can passively diffuse back into the blood, reducing net elimination.
Kidney: the dominant route for most drugs and metabolites.
Bile / feces: important for some large or protein-bound drugs.
Lungs: volatile agents (e.g., anesthetic gases).
Sweat / breast milk: minor routes, but breast milk matters for lactating patients.
**Decreased renal function → decreased drug clearance → increased drug exposure and accumulation risk.**

For a primarily renally eliminated drug when eGFR drops: decrease the dose and/or extend the dosing interval, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
Urine pH manipulation (e.g., alkalinizing urine in aspirin overdose) works by trapping ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption.

t: Why does alkalinizing urine help in aspirin overdose? It keeps the drug ionized in the tubule, and only un-ionized drug can diffuse back — so reabsorption is blocked and more drug leaves.
Why adjust doses in CKD? Less renal function → less clearance → more exposure and accumulation of renally-cleared drugs.
Kidney handling = "**F**ilter, **S**ecrete, **R**eabsorb" — **F**ree drug filtered, **S**ecreted by transporters, **R**eabsorbed if lipophilic & un-ionized.
**Half-life (t½) = the time required for the plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%.**
**Steady state:** the point at which drug intake equals drug elimination; reached in about 4–5 half-lives with regular dosing.
**Loading dose:** a larger initial dose used to rapidly reach a therapeutic concentration, without waiting for steady state.
**Maintenance dose:** the regular, ongoing dose that keeps the drug within the therapeutic range once steady state is reached.
**Clearance = the volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time.**
**t½ = 0.7 × Vd / CL** — half-life rises when Vd rises or clearance falls.
**Loading dose = Vd × target concentration** (e.g., theophylline: 35 L × 10 mg/L = 350 mg for a 70-kg adult).
**Extraction ratio:** the share of drug the liver removes in one pass. High-ER drugs have low oral bioavailability (morphine ER 0.67 → about 33%).
**Target concentration approach** (the rational way to design a dosage regimen): pick the level that gives the desired effect, then dose from the patient’s clearance and Vd.
**Zero-order absorption** runs at a constant rate (controlled-release forms); **first-order** is proportional to the amount left.
PK calculations = the math PAs actually use at the bedside.
Half-life is determined by clearance and volume of distribution together — it is not a fixed drug "property" independent of physiology.
A drug is roughly 97% eliminated after about 5 half-lives.
**Formula: % remaining = 100% x (1/2)^(number of half-life)** — i.e., per number of half-lives elapsed.
**Formula: C(t) = C₀ x (1/2)^(t/t½)** — C₀ = starting concentration, t = time elapsed.
Worked example (both formulas): t½ = 6 h; an IV dose gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L — see the table for each half-life.
Clearance determines how efficiently a drug is removed — and, along with Vd, determines half-life.
Total clearance is usually the sum of hepatic and renal clearance.
Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance.
Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives regardless of dose size — the same reason a drug is ~97% eliminated ~5 half-lives after stopping it.
Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.
During regular dosing: 50% of steady state after 1 half-life, 75% after 2, and over 90% after 4 — the textbook's "four half-lives" rule of thumb.
**Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination:** clearance falls as concentration rises — important for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin.
**Maintenance dosing rate = clearance × target concentration** (÷ F if oral). The dosing interval changes only peaks and troughs, not the average level.
Half-life can change without clearance changing: diazepam’s half-life lengthens with age because its Vd grows.
Effects can outlast plasma levels (delayed effects): warfarin acts only as clotting factors turn over.

Case: significant CKD + a medication primarily eliminated unchanged by the kidney. **What happens to the drug's concentration and half-life, and would you adjust the dose, the dosing interval, or both?**

**Clinical pearl:** reduced clearance raises drug concentration and prolongs half-life; many renally-cleared drugs are managed by extending the dosing interval, reducing the dose, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
The logic chain: clearance ↓ → half-life ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation risk ↑ if the regimen is not adjusted.
Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life.
A loading dose reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives; it does not change the maintenance dose or remove the need for monitoring.
High-extraction drugs (morphine, propranolol, verapamil) vary widely between patients, and far more drug gets through in cirrhosis.
**Schedule matters:** gentamicin is more nephrotoxic as a constant infusion than as intermittent doses at the same average level.
Give IV loading doses slowly (over an hour): a fast bolus can overshoot into toxicity, e.g., phenytoin.
Timing drug levels: digoxin at least 6 hours after the dose; lithium just before the next dose.
In obesity, dose drugs that stay out of fat (gentamicin, digoxin) on fat-free mass.
Displacing a drug from plasma proteins raises free drug only briefly; the body eliminates the extra, so binding changes rarely matter clinically.

From concepts to clinical decisions: one integrated pharmacology pathway — Dose → Absorption → Distribution → Receptor / Target → Effect, with Metabolism and Excretion clearing the drug.

CYP interaction in action: a patient stable on a CYP3A4-substrate medication starts a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. **What happens to the first drug's level, and what would you watch for clinically?**
**Clinical pearl: always check for CYP450 interactions before adding a new drug to an existing regimen — one of the most preventable causes of toxicity.**

Agonist or antagonist? A new drug binds the same receptor as a home medication, and the home medication's effect weakens. **Is the new drug most likely a competitive antagonist, and how could you confirm it pharmacologically?**

**Clinical pearl: a competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — if raising the home medication's dose restores the effect, that supports competitive (rather than irreversible) antagonism.**

Study-guide case: 68-year-old woman, stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min), starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney; she started a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor 3 weeks ago.

Two concerns: reduced renal clearance from CKD will raise the antiarrhythmic's concentration and prolong its half-life regardless of the new drug; separately, if it has any hepatic/CYP3A4 component, the CYP3A4 inhibitor would compound accumulation further.

Before dispensing: check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and closely monitor renal function and signs of toxicity (arrhythmia worsening, other drug-specific toxicity) after starting.

If the drug were instead cleared by the liver via CYP3A4: the direct renal-clearance concern becomes less central (though CKD can still indirectly affect hepatic drug handling), and the CYP3A4 interaction becomes the dominant concern.

L03 · Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Session 1 — study guide
**Nociceptive pain:** direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
**Neuropathic pain:** pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
**Chronic pain:** persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.
**Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**
Key mediators: **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).**
Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
**NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.**
**Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂** (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
**Nociceptor sensitization:** injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which **lower the pain threshold** — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.
Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target; bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.
Where drugs act: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.
**The immune response:** chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.
Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.
The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

**Therapeutic strategies:** goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.
Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.

Combining acetaminophen with an NSAID improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.
Normal handling: acetaminophen → NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione conjugation → safe excretion.
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — the “toxic metabolite” example from Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism section.
**Major route (~90%):** glucuronidation and sulfation → safe urinary excretion.
**Minor route (~5–10%):** CYP2E1 oxidation → NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine), normally neutralized by glutathione (GSH) conjugation at therapeutic doses.
Mostly conjugated to inactive sulfate and glucuronide; half-life 2–3 hours, relatively unaffected by renal function.
**Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**
Patients often don’t realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label — reinforce generic-name awareness.
**Acute single ingestion:** plot the acetaminophen level on the **Rumack-Matthew nomogram**; check AST/ALT.
**How to use the nomogram:** draw a level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it against time since ingestion.
**Above the treatment line:** give NAC. **Below the line:** toxicity unlikely. Example: 8 h, 120 mcg/mL is above the line, so start NAC.
The illustrative treatment line runs from 150 mcg/mL at 4 h, halving every 4 h, to 4.7 mcg/mL at 24 h.
**Limits:** not valid before 4 hours, with an unknown ingestion time, or for staggered, repeated supratherapeutic, or chronic ingestion — use clinical judgment, AST/ALT, and poison control.
Start NAC without waiting if presentation is late or the level is unavailable and the ingestion is significant.
After 24 hours the nomogram is not used: 4.7 mcg/mL is only where the treatment line ends, not a safe cutoff. A detectable level or elevated AST/ALT guides NAC, per protocol or poison control.
Adults: generally no more than 4 g/day — and even 4 g is associated with more liver function test abnormalities.
**Antidote: N-acetylcysteine**, a glutathione precursor — it replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
Case: a patient on regular acetaminophen for back pain starts an OTC cold-and-flu combination. **What is the hidden danger in this combination?** Double-dosing acetaminophen.
**Antidote: NAC (N-acetylcysteine) replenishes glutathione; give early for best effect.**
Ask: “What is the danger of a cold-and-flu product on top of regular acetaminophen?” Look for unintentional double dosing from combination products.
**Other analgesics — tramadol:** weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; no anti-inflammatory effect; up to 300 mg/day; risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.

t: NSAID → COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, inflammation, fever.
**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.
**COX-2:** induced mainly at sites of inflammation and the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins; selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity.
Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
**Pathway:** COX converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins **and thromboxane A2 (TXA2)**. Less prostaglandin: pain, fever, and inflammation fall. Less TXA2: bleeding risk.
Every NSAID shares the COX mechanism; the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins (GI injury, platelet inhibition, renal effects).
**COX-1 is constitutive:** gastric mucosa (protection), platelets (TXA2, clotting), kidney (renal blood flow). **COX-2 is inducible** in inflamed tissue: pain, swelling, fever.
Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms, so GI injury is common. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.
Celecoxib selectively inhibits inducible COX-2, the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins, and largely spares COX-1 in gastric mucosa — lowering ulcer and bleeding risk.
**Celecoxib’s trade-off:** PGI2 (prostacyclin) falls without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular event risk; stomach and platelet protection continue.
Celecoxib still affects kidney prostaglandins, so renal risk is not eliminated.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.
Oral NSAIDs for osteoarthritis — effective, but carry the systemic risks below.
Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure.
NSAIDs ease symptoms but, unlike DMARDs, do not alter the course of any arthritic disorder.
Used in RA, spondyloarthropathies, OA, sprains and strains, low back pain, and gout (tolmetin appears ineffective in gout).
**Gastrointestinal:** gastritis, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding.

Also caution or avoid with anticoagulant therapy and in late pregnancy.
Ibuprofen is relatively contraindicated with nasal polyps, angioedema, or bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin.
NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk; add a diuretic and it is the **“triple whammy,”** a very high-yield AKI pattern.
NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk.
NSAIDs + corticosteroids → ↑ GI ulcer risk.
Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
Celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin and raises lithium and fluconazole levels.
Naproxen’s longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; diclofenac comes as oral and topical forms.
**Chemistry & pharmacokinetics:** most NSAIDs are weak acids, well absorbed, ~98% albumin-bound, metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2C, and renally excreted.
These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion (Table 1).
Highest GI-bleeding risk: celecoxib, or a nonselective NSAID plus omeprazole or misoprostol.
Case: a 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant. **Is an NSAID a good first-line choice for this patient’s pain? Why or why not?**
**Three NSAID red flags at once** — renal disease, anticoagulation, and age-related bleeding risk — make acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy generally safer first-line.
Celecoxib is a classic “trade one risk for another” point: a better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.
There is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.
**Choice of NSAID:** all are about equally effective, so choose by toxicity, cost, and patient factors; in renal insufficiency nonacetylated salicylates may be best.

t: Why do NSAIDs hurt the stomach and kidney? Blocking COX-1, the housekeeping enzyme, removes the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa and keep renal blood flow normal.
Why the “triple whammy”? An ACE inhibitor/ARB, a diuretic, and an NSAID each push kidney perfusion the wrong way at once — together they cause acute kidney injury.
NSAID harms = **GRC**: **G**ut, **R**enal, **C**ardiovascular (Table 1).
**Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
**OA pathophysiology:** mechanical load and wear degrade cartilage; bone remodels with osteophytes.
**RA pathophysiology:** immune activation → autoimmune synovitis forms a **pannus** that erodes cartilage and bone; **TNF-α and IL-6** drive the inflammation and joint damage.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
**NSAIDs** relieve pain and swelling within days but do not alter joint damage; **DMARDs** take weeks to months to act, then slow cartilage and bone destruction.
**Timing:** judge a DMARD over months, not after the first visit — set expectations that benefit builds over months. Relief now with NSAIDs, protection later with DMARDs.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.
**Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens.**

t: **Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.** (methotrexate)
**Hydroxychloroquine** alters lysosomal and TLR signaling (less antigen signaling); **sulfasalazine** reduces cytokine and prostaglandin production.
**Leflunomide** inhibits DHODH, blocking pyrimidine synthesis (slower T-cell growth).
Conventional DMARDs act inside cells or on broad immune pathways, with a slower onset than biologics.
**Methotrexate’s folate pathway:** blocking DHFR stops dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF), the folate needed for purine and thymidylate (DNA) synthesis.
At low RA doses methotrexate is likely anti-inflammatory via **adenosine release**, not cytotoxicity.
TNF inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha signaling.
IL-6 inhibitors block interleukin-6 receptor signaling.
B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
**TNF inhibitors:** antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab) and etanercept, a receptor fusion protein, neutralize soluble and membrane TNF-α, preventing TNFR activation.
**Tocilizumab** blocks both membrane and soluble IL-6 receptors.
**Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig)** binds CD80/86 and blocks CD28 costimulation, acting early at T-cell activation.
**Rituximab (anti-CD20)** binds CD20 and depletes B cells for months.
Each biologic intercepts a different step of the immune cascade: walk it from T-cell activation to cytokines to synovial damage — abatacept acts earliest.
**OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
**Where each OA analgesic acts:** acetaminophen centrally (brain and spinal cord COX) — little anti-inflammatory effect in the joint.
Oral or topical NSAIDs block COX in joint tissue (synovium and cartilage), lowering prostaglandins, pain, and swelling.
An intra-articular steroid calms local inflammation inside the joint for fast, short-term flare relief. Choice depends on which tissue drives the pain.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
TNF inhibitors are the first-line biologic; tocilizumab works as monotherapy; rituximab is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.
**Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.

t: **Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).**
Don’t stack biologics: abatacept with a TNF inhibitor probably raises serious infections; upadacitinib with biologic DMARDs is not recommended.
Hydroxychloroquine can reduce methotrexate clearance.
Tocilizumab stimulates CYP450 — doses of cyclosporine or warfarin may need adjusting.
Methotrexate given with TNF inhibitors reduces anti-drug antibodies (infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab).
**Methotrexate is dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**
**Weekly dosing only:** daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity.
**Folate supplementation** is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce toxicity.
Folic acid co-therapy reduces methotrexate’s liver, marrow, lung, and GI toxicity.
**Baseline screening:** e.g., tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening before starting biologics.
**Vaccination:** update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting therapy.
**Ongoing monitoring:** regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
**Infection precautions:** counsel patients to report fevers or infection symptoms promptly.
**Screen first:** TB test (IGRA or TST) and hepatitis B and C serology before starting; check hepatitis B before rituximab.
**Vaccines:** update non-live vaccines before treatment.
**Monitor:** CBC and liver and kidney labs every 1–3 months; act early on fever or infection signs.
Folic acid or leucovorin reduces stomatitis, GI, and liver test problems but may cut methotrexate efficacy by 10–18%.
Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye exam, then annual screening after 5 years (retinopathy).
Avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after stopping abatacept; stop upadacitinib before a live attenuated vaccine.
A 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant: acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy first.
OA and RA both affect the joint but are two very different diseases — don’t give RA patients analgesia alone.
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety points in all of rheumatology pharmacology.
Match each generic name to its class: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (TNF); tocilizumab (IL-6); rituximab (B cell); abatacept (T-cell costimulation).

**Read the stem first:** it reveals the mechanism class before the drug is recalled (-mab antibody: -zumab humanized, -ximab chimeric, -umab fully human; -cept receptor fusion; -nib/-tinib kinase inhibitor; -coxib COX-2 selective; -profen, -fenac, -oxicam NSAID subclasses).
Topical diclofenac 1% gel is sold over the counter for OA and muscular pain.
**Biosimilars:** near-copies of legacy biologics with the same efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity at potentially lower cost.
If methotrexate alone falls short: add csDMARDs or a biologic — usually a TNF inhibitor first, then non-TNF biologics or JAK inhibitors.

Gout is a crystal-driven inflammatory arthritis with **two very different treatment phases**.

**The chain:** purine metabolism → uric acid → monosodium urate crystals → joint inflammation. Everything downstream — colchicine, allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid — targets a specific point along this chain.
**Purine breakdown:** hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (via **xanthine oxidase**) → hyperuricemia → urate crystals in the joint.
Crystals activate neutrophils and macrophages (**NLRP3, IL-1β**) → the acute flare, the end of the cascade.
**Raise urate:** diets rich in purines and fructose; alcohol, especially beer (more production, less renal excretion).
**Lower urate excretion:** diuretics, especially thiazides and loop agents; chronic kidney disease sustains hyperuricemia.

Walk the full chain and sort the drugs into **two buckets:** “lowers uric acid” (allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid) vs. “treats the acute flare” (colchicine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids) — the same acute-vs-chronic distinction made explicit next.
**Acute flare** — goal: control pain and inflammation now. Agents: colchicine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids.
**Chronic management** — goal: lower serum uric acid to prevent future flares. Agents: allopurinol, febuxostat (↓ production); probenecid (↑ excretion).
Humans lack uricase, the enzyme other mammals use to turn uric acid into soluble allantoin; most people with hyperuricemia never have a gout attack.
Treat gout, not a number: long-term drug treatment of asymptomatic hyperuricemia is unproven. Adherence is poor (18–26% in younger patients).
Colchicine — acute treatment (plant-derived alkaloid, no stem).

t: **Mechanism: disrupts microtubule formation in neutrophils.** Colchicine binds tubulin → less neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation → less inflammation at the crystal site.
Colchicine works on the cell’s cytoskeleton, so its effect builds in the early hours of a flare.
**Allopurinol** (via its metabolite oxypurinol) and **febuxostat** block **xanthine oxidase** → ↓ uric acid **production**.
Febuxostat is also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, with a different chemical structure.
**Probenecid — mechanism: inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid, increasing its excretion** (blocks URAT1). A uricosuric, not a xanthine oxidase inhibitor — a different strategy.
**Pegloticase, rasburicase:** recombinant **uricase** converts uric acid to **allantoin**, which is soluble and excreted.
Uricosurics block reabsorption; uricases remove uric acid enzymatically, which is why they suit refractory disease.
NSAIDs and corticosteroids reduce joint inflammation in a flare.
Allopurinol is a purine analog; its metabolite oxypurinol (half-life 15 hours) also inhibits xanthine oxidase, so it is dosed once daily.
Colchicine relieves gout pain and inflammation in 12–24 hours without changing urate metabolism or excretion.
Glucocorticoids in gout: reduce neutrophil migration, prostaglandins, and IL-1β.
**Treat the acute flare first** (colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid); urate-lowering therapy is deferred until the flare resolves, then used for long-term prevention.
Colchicine is most effective when started early in a flare — **best within 24 hours of onset**.
Allopurinol is first-line for most patients; febuxostat is the alternative when allopurinol is not tolerated or contraindicated.
Probenecid is an older, second-line oral option. **Pegloticase — a recombinant uricase enzyme for severe, refractory gout not controlled by other agents.**

Corticosteroids are a good alternative when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated, including CKD: prednisone 30–50 mg/d for 1–2 days, tapered over 7–10 days, or intra-articular.

Different mechanisms for **spasm, spasticity, and rigidity** — not the same thing, and they often require distinct pharmacologic approaches.
**Muscle spasm:** sudden, involuntary contraction, often from acute musculoskeletal injury; typically treated with centrally acting relaxants.
**Spasticity:** velocity-dependent increased tone from **upper motor neuron injury**. **Rigidity:** constant increased tone, independent of velocity.

**Where tone is controlled:** upper motor neurons (descending inhibitory pathways) ▸ spinal interneurons (GABA, glycine, alpha-2) ▸ alpha motor neuron ▸ neuromuscular junction (ACh release) ▸ muscle fiber contraction (SR Ca²⁺ release).
**Centrally acting** (act within the CNS to reduce muscle tone): cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, baclofen — first-line; carisoprodol, methocarbamol, metaxalone, chlorzoxazone — other options.

**Peripherally / locally acting:** dantrolene acts directly on skeletal muscle itself; botulinum toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction — useful when a central mechanism is not desired (or not safe).
**Highest-yield distinction:** “where does the drug act?” sorts every agent into one of two buckets — **dantrolene is the only one in the peripheral (muscle) bucket.**
Spasticity is common after spinal injury, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, and stroke; these drugs relieve painful spasm better than they restore function.

t: **Central agents** reduce CNS excitatory output to motor neurons → ↓ muscle tone. Baclofen and tizanidine act on spinal interneurons and afferents; cyclobenzaprine acts in the brainstem.

**Baclofen — mechanism: GABA-B receptor agonist in the spinal cord.** Binding GABA-B → opens K⁺ channels, closes Ca²⁺ channels (presynaptic inhibition) → less excitatory transmitter release → lower motor neuron firing → reduced spasticity.
**Tizanidine — mechanism: central α2-adrenergic agonist.** Activating alpha-2 receptors → reduced presynaptic release of excitatory amino acids → lower motor neuron activity → reduced muscle tone.

**Cyclobenzaprine:** acts in the brainstem; antagonizes **5-HT2** and descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways → reduced tonic somatic motor activity → muscle relaxation. Structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants.

**Dantrolene — mechanism: decreases calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum.** Nerve impulse → DHPR activated → **RyR1** opens → Ca²⁺ released → contraction; dantrolene blocks RyR1 → less Ca²⁺ → relaxation.

t: Dantrolene acts inside the fiber on RyR1 — directly on the muscle fiber, not the CNS — distinct from every centrally acting agent.

**Botulinum toxin — blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction** (ACh release at the junction) — a third mechanism, distinct from both CNS-acting drugs and dantrolene’s sarcoplasmic-reticulum action.
Diazepam (GABA-A) reduces spasticity partly in the spinal cord, but sedates at the doses needed.
Dantrolene binds RyR1; cardiac and smooth muscle use RyR2, so they are minimally depressed.
**Baclofen:** spasticity, particularly from spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis; intrathecal option for severe spasticity.
Cyclobenzaprine — **primary use: short-term treatment of acute, localized muscle spasm**; short-term use only, 2–3 weeks.

Dantrolene — **clinical use #1: malignant hyperthermia (a true emergency indication)** (triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine) — a true emergency, perioperative indication where the drug is literally life-saving.
**Dantrolene #2:** chronic spasticity, when central agents are not appropriate; also used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome. IV formulation for acute crisis.
**Botulinum toxin:** focal spasticity or dystonia; effect is local and temporary, requiring repeat injections.
Malignant hyperthermia: give IV dantrolene 1 mg/kg, repeated as needed, while controlling acidosis and temperature.
Cyclobenzaprine is ineffective for spasm from cerebral palsy or spinal cord injury.
Gabapentin has shown promise as a spasmolytic in multiple sclerosis.
Botulinum toxin: black box warning for distant spread of toxin, greatest in children treated for spasticity.

t: Why is dantrolene the malignant hyperthermia drug? MH is runaway calcium release through RyR1 in muscle; a CNS drug can’t reach that — dantrolene blocks RyR1 itself.
Why does stopping intrathecal baclofen go badly? The spinal cord loses its GABA-B brake all at once: seizures, hyperthermia, and rebound spasticity.
**Cyclobenzaprine looks like a tricyclic, acts like one:** sleepy, dry, can’t pee, confused — and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.
Bone pharmacology is about **balancing bone formation and bone resorption**.
**Osteoblasts** build new bone matrix (promoted by several osteoporosis therapies); **osteoclasts** resorb existing bone (suppressed by most osteoporosis therapies).
Nearly every osteoporosis drug shifts this balance one way or the other — slowing osteoclasts or stimulating osteoblasts.
**RANKL/OPG:** osteoblasts or stromal cells express RANKL → RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast differentiation and activation → bone resorption releases calcium.
**OPG** is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL. Estrogen increases OPG; denosumab mimics OPG. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling in osteoblasts.
**PTH:** intermittent dosing favors formation; continuous exposure raises RANKL and resorption.

**Calcium homeostasis:** PTH raises serum calcium (mobilizes bone calcium when levels drop); vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption; calcitonin lowers serum calcium and opposes PTH; calcium is the substrate being regulated (intake, bone storage, excretion).

**PTH feedback loop:** falling serum calcium → PTH → raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption; restored calcium inhibits further PTH.
**Risk factors:** aging; estrogen deficiency (e.g., postmenopausal status); **chronic glucocorticoid use**; low calcium or vitamin D intake; low physical activity.
About 98% of the body’s calcium is in bone; PTH, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D are the principal regulators.
Excess endogenous PTH nets bone resorption, but low intermittent doses build bone first — the basis for teriparatide.
Glucocorticoids block vitamin D–driven gut calcium transport, raise renal calcium loss, block formation, and initially stimulate resorption.
Alendronate — oral bisphosphonate (first-line).

t: Bisphosphonates — **mechanism: inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.** They bind hydroxyapatite at resorption sites → osteoclasts take them up → nitrogen-containing agents inhibit **FPP synthase** (mevalonate pathway) → loss of prenylation of small GTPases → **osteoclast apoptosis**.
**Denosumab:** monoclonal antibody, **RANKL inhibitor** — blocks osteoclast formation.
**Teriparatide** (PTH 1-34, daily injection) / **abaloparatide:** PTH-analog “anabolic” agents that stimulate osteoblasts and new bone formation.
**Romosozumab:** sclerostin antibody that both builds bone and limits resorption — increases formation, decreases resorption → BMD up, fracture risk down.
**SERMs** — selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene): estrogen-like effect on bone — antiresorptive, like calcitonin.
**Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis:** glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven formation.
Amino-bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway.
Denosumab does not kill osteoclasts and does not deposit in bone, so its effect reverses when stopped.
**Bisphosphonates are first-line for most patients with osteoporosis.**
Higher-risk patients may need an **anabolic agent first**.
Raloxifene also reduces breast cancer risk.
Raloxifene protects against spine fractures but not hip fractures; bisphosphonates, denosumab, and teriparatide protect both.
Vitamin D (800 IU/d) with calcium improves bone density, reduces falls, and prevents fractures — the base under every osteoporosis drug.
Calcitonin is less effective (spine fractures only); bisphosphonates and calcitonin are first-line for Paget disease.
**Romosozumab: boxed warning for MI, stroke, and cardiovascular death.**

t: Bisphosphonates: contraindicated with severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30–35 mL/min) — some are avoided in significant renal impairment.
Oral bisphosphonates: avoid in esophageal stricture, achalasia, or inability to sit upright.
Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab can be used in advanced renal disease (not renally cleared) — watch calcium.
Food, calcium, coffee, and antacids reduce oral bisphosphonate absorption further.
Bisphosphonates have a long skeletal half-life — the effect persists after stopping.
Poor oral absorption (under 1%) → take fasting with plain water.
**Dosing:** alendronate, risedronate — oral, typically weekly; ibandronate — oral, monthly; zoledronic acid — IV, as infrequently as once yearly.
Teriparatide is limited to 2 years lifetime, then follow with an antiresorptive.
Bisphosphonates: less than 10% of an oral dose is absorbed; about half goes to bone, the rest is excreted unchanged in urine.
Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months; teriparatide 20 mcg SC daily; romosozumab 210 mg SC monthly for one year, then an antiresorptive.

**Oral counseling:** take with a **full glass of water**, first thing in the morning, on an empty stomach well before food, and **remain upright** (sitting or standing) for the specified period after dosing (30 minutes).
Ensure calcium and vitamin D repletion before starting; correct hypocalcemia first.
Consider a **drug holiday after 3–5 years** of oral therapy (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femur fracture with long-term use).
Reassess after 5 years of bisphosphonate (3 for zoledronate); a drug holiday if fracture risk allows.
The “remain upright” point is extremely high-yield: esophageal injury is largely preventable with correct administration.
**Can’t swallow pills?** Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable (e.g., denosumab) avoids the oral route.
Dosing frequency is a major real-world driver of which bisphosphonate a patient actually takes consistently.
Teriparatide, abaloparatide, and romosozumab are the **anabolic exception** — they actively build new bone; most other osteoporosis drugs just slow resorption.
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis is especially high-yield — it connects to the corticosteroid use for OA/RA in Session 1.

**Choosing therapy:** fracture risk, renal function, previous fracture history, glucocorticoid exposure, adherence (weekly oral vs. yearly IV vs. injectable), and route preference. This checklist is a direct echo of Lecture 1’s clinical decision-making framework.

Applying the whole musculoskeletal pharmacology toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line drug class AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing it.
**1.** Pain and inflammation are related but distinct — treat them accordingly.
**2.** NSAIDs are effective for pain and inflammation, but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk.
**3.** DMARDs modify the underlying disease process in RA — they do more than mask symptoms.
**4.** Acute gout treatment and chronic urate-lowering therapy are different goals, started at different times.
**5.** Bone pharmacology is fundamentally about the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity.
Every mechanism here — COX inhibition, CYP interactions, renal dosing, pharmacogenomics — is Lecture 1’s toolkit applied to one organ system.

**Patient D — postmenopausal osteoporosis, high fracture risk:** consider an anabolic agent first; check its limits (teriparatide 2 years; romosozumab CV boxed warning).

Gout runs **purine → uric acid (xanthine oxidase) → urate crystals → neutrophil flare**; treat the **flare** with colchicine, an NSAID, or a corticosteroid, and **never start urate-lowering therapy during a flare**.

**Allopurinol/febuxostat** cut uric acid production (xanthine oxidase), **probenecid** raises excretion (URAT1), and **pegloticase** breaks uric acid down — watch HLA-B*58:01, febuxostat’s CV boxed warning, and G6PD deficiency.
Muscle relaxants sort by site: **central** (baclofen GABA-B, tizanidine α2, cyclobenzaprine brainstem) vs. **peripheral** (**dantrolene** on RyR1 in muscle; botulinum toxin at the junction).

**Dantrolene** is the emergency drug for **malignant hyperthermia**; never stop intrathecal **baclofen** abruptly; check **LFTs** and CYP1A2 inhibitors with tizanidine; cyclobenzaprine is anticholinergic (Beers).

Bone is a **balance**: PTH answers low calcium via bone, kidney, and gut; **bisphosphonates** (first-line), **denosumab**, raloxifene, and calcitonin slow resorption, while **teriparatide/abaloparatide** and **romosozumab** build bone.
Oral bisphosphonates need a **full glass of water, fasting, and 30 minutes upright**; denosumab must not just be stopped, teriparatide is 2 years, and romosozumab carries an MI/stroke boxed warning.

Acid-peptic disease is **a balance between mucosal defense and acid-driven aggression**.
**Aggressive factors:** gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).
**Protective (mucosal defense) factors:** mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.
**GERD:** reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.
**Peptic ulcer disease (PUD):** a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
**Gastritis:** inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).
Over 90% of peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs; bile also counts as an aggressive factor.

Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.
**NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins**, removing mucosal protection — the clearest example of tipping the balance.
**H. pylori urease makes ammonia**, which injures the mucosa.
**Stress and critical illness raise the risk of stress ulceration.**
**Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) causes severe acid hypersecretion.**
**Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump.** H2 blockers cut one input (histamine); PPIs block the last step itself.

**Physiology of acid secretion:** gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.
GERD, PUD and gastritis share the same drug toolkit: reduce acid, protect the mucosa, and/or eradicate H. pylori.
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.

t: **Antacids — mechanism: directly neutralize existing gastric acid (do not reduce acid production).** **Acid in stomach** → **antacid base (Al/Mg hydroxide, calcium carbonate) neutralizes H+** → **higher gastric pH** → rapid but short relief.

**H2RAs — mechanism: competitively block histamine at the H2 receptor on parietal cells.** Histamine from ECL cells → H2 receptor → cAMP rises → stimulates the proton pump; famotidine occupies the receptor competitively, so less acid.
**PPIs — mechanism: irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the final common pathway of acid secretion.**
**PPI prodrug activated by acid** → **binds H⁺/K⁺ ATPase irreversibly** → **final step of acid secretion blocked**.

Pathway: enteric-coated prodrug absorbed in the small intestine → reaches the parietal cell canaliculus → activated by acid → binds a cysteine on H⁺/K⁺-ATPase covalently → **pump irreversibly blocked until new pumps are made**.
PPIs achieve substantially greater acid-suppression potency and longer duration of effect than H2RAs (Figure 4: potency 95 vs. 45; duration 90 vs. 50, illustrative).
H2 blockers inhibit 60–70% of 24-hour acid secretion; PPIs inhibit 90–98% because they block the final common pathway.
**Antacids:** onset is rapid, but duration is short — best for intermittent, mild symptom relief.
**H2RAs:** mild-to-moderate GERD, maintenance therapy, adjunct for peptic ulcer healing; best at controlling **nocturnal** acid.
**PPIs:** first-line for GERD, PUD healing, and H. pylori regimens.
Infrequent heartburn (fewer than three times per week): antacids or as-needed H2 blockers; antacids act faster but last 1–2 hours vs. 6–10 hours.
PPIs heal over 90% of duodenal ulcers within 4 weeks; GERD recurs in over 80% within 6 months of stopping.
Stress-related bleeding prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients: an oral PPI if enteral meds are possible, otherwise IV H2 blocker or PPI.

**PPI long-term adverse effects: vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, increased fracture risk, and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection** — also pneumonia and acute interstitial nephritis.

Magnesium and aluminum antacids are renally excreted: avoid long-term use in renal insufficiency.
**Antacids can impair absorption of many other oral drugs — separate dosing by at least 2 hours.** They bind levothyroxine, quinolones, tetracyclines, and iron.
**Omeprazole (a CYP2C19 inhibitor) can reduce clopidogrel activation, blunting its antiplatelet effect.** Omeprazole and esomeprazole both inhibit CYP2C19.
**Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4)** — a callback to Lecture 1: it raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.
Famotidine has minimal CYP450 interaction.
Antacids should not be given within 2 hours of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, itraconazole, and iron.
With clopidogrel, prefer pantoprazole or rabeprazole (minimal CYP2C19 inhibition).
Less acid lowers absorption of ketoconazole, itraconazole, digoxin, and atazanavir.
**PPIs are best absorbed/effective when taken 30–60 minutes before a meal** (timed to peak pump activity) — they work best on actively secreting pumps.
CYP2C19 genotype alters PPI exposure; ultrarapid metabolizers may need higher doses.
Famotidine needs renal dose adjustment.
PPIs: food cuts bioavailability by about 50%; half-life about 1.5 hours yet acid inhibition lasts up to 24 hours; full effect takes 3–4 days.
PPIs need no renal dose reduction; consider reduction in severe liver impairment.
Many patients stay on PPIs far longer than necessary — the long-term adverse-effect list drives deprescribing conversations.
Ask: what happens to warfarin or phenytoin levels if cimetidine is added? They rise (CYP inhibition).

t: **Sucralfate:** in acid (pH below 4) it polymerizes, binds the ulcer base and **forms a protective barrier**; requires an acidic environment to activate; minimal systemic absorption.
**Misoprostol:** **a prostaglandin E1 analog** — acts on EP receptors to reduce acid and increase mucus and bicarbonate, **restoring the protective prostaglandin tone that NSAIDs suppress**.
**Why H. pylori needs multiple drugs:** it lives in gastric mucus and buffers acid with urease-made ammonia.

A PPI raises gastric pH so bacteria enter a replicating state and antibiotics are more stable; amoxicillin blocks cell wall synthesis; clarithromycin (50S ribosome) or metronidazole adds a second antibiotic.
Sucralfate is sucrose complexed to sulfated aluminum hydroxide; less than 3% is absorbed.
Bismuth coats ulcers, has direct antimicrobial effects and binds enterotoxins (traveler’s diarrhea).
**Triple therapy:** PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 10–14 days (usual duration 14 days).

**Bismuth quadruple therapy:** PPI (or H2RA) + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline — preferred where clarithromycin resistance is a concern, with recent macrolide exposure, or with penicillin allergy.
**Penicillin allergy:** substitute metronidazole for amoxicillin in triple therapy.
