t: **5-HT3 antagonists** block serotonin at gut vagal afferents/CTZ.

Chemotherapy or gut irritation damages enterochromaffin cells → serotonin binds 5-HT3 on vagal afferents and the CTZ → signal to the vomiting center; **ondansetron blocks 5-HT3, so no signal reaches the vomiting center**.
**D2 antagonists** block dopamine at the CTZ (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine).
**NK1 antagonists** block substance P/neurokinin at the CTZ (aprepitant).
**H1/M1 antagonists** block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (meclizine, scopolamine).

**Metoclopramide — mechanism: D2 antagonism (antiemetic effect) plus enhancement of upper-GI motility (prokinetic effect).** D2 blockade in the CTZ → less nausea; D2 blockade plus **5-HT4 agonism** in the gut → more acetylcholine → faster gastric emptying.
Dronabinol (CB1 agonist) crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center, CTZ and hypothalamus, reducing neurotransmitter release → less nausea, more appetite.
Mechanism is distinct from the four pathways (5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1).
**Pathophysiology of vomiting:** the vomiting center sits in the lateral medullary reticular formation; the CTZ (area postrema) lies outside the blood-brain barrier.
Ondansetron: give before chemotherapy; oral ODT and IV forms are available.
**Metoclopramide clinical uses: nausea/vomiting and diabetic gastroparesis.**

**Dronabinol — a synthetic cannabinoid (CB1 receptor agonist) used for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and appetite stimulation.** Typically reserved for patients who do not respond adequately to standard antiemetics.
**Chemotherapy:** combine classes with different targets — a 5-HT3 antagonist, an NK1 antagonist, and dexamethasone; avoid duplicating the same mechanism.
**Match drug to cause:** gut/vagal triggers respond to 5-HT3 antagonists; the CTZ to D2 or NK1 antagonists.
5-HT3 antagonists control vagal and chemotherapy emesis but poorly control motion sickness; palonosetron also prevents delayed emesis.
**Pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics (5-HT3):** first-generation agents have half-lives of 4–9 hours; palonosetron 40 hours; no dose cut in renal insufficiency.
NK1 antagonist + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone prevents acute emesis in 80–90% of highly emetogenic chemotherapy patients.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) prevent anticipatory vomiting before chemotherapy.
Metoclopramide — **boxed warning: risk of tardive dyskinesia, particularly with prolonged use or high doses — limit duration of therapy.** Avoid beyond 12 weeks.

Acid-peptic disease is a **balance**: acid, pepsin, H. pylori and NSAIDs push against mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins and epithelial turnover.
Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine converge on the **proton pump**: **H2 blockers** cut one input, **PPIs** block the final common pathway, **antacids** neutralize acid already made.
PPIs are the most potent but carry long-term risks — **B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile** — and omeprazole blunts **clopidogrel** via CYP2C19.
**Sucralfate** shields the ulcer base (needs acid); **misoprostol** restores prostaglandins for NSAID-ulcer prevention but is **contraindicated in pregnancy**.
**H. pylori** needs eradication: triple therapy, or **bismuth quadruple** with penicillin allergy, recent macrolide, or clarithromycin resistance; test of cure ≥ 4 weeks later, off the PPI 2 weeks.

Antiemetics block one input to the vomiting center: **5-HT3** (ondansetron), **D2** (metoclopramide — boxed tardive dyskinesia), **NK1** (aprepitant), **H1/M1** (meclizine, scopolamine — motion sickness), plus **CB1** (dronabinol).

t: L06 · GI & Nutrition Pharmacology — Session 2 — study guide
**Opposite problems, each with its own family of mechanisms.** Four laxative buckets: bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, secretagogue — sort any laxative name into one of them.
**Bulk-forming** (psyllium, methylcellulose): absorb water, increase stool bulk and transit; slowest onset; generally safest for long-term use.
**Osmotic** (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium hydroxide): draw water into the lumen; fast, reliable onset.
**Stimulant** (senna, bisacodyl): directly stimulate enteric nerves/motility; reserve for short-term or breakthrough use.
**Secretagogues** (lubiprostone, linaclotide): increase intestinal chloride and fluid secretion; used for chronic constipation, IBS-C.
Polyethylene glycol 3350 — osmotic; first-line for chronic constipation.

t: Laxative mechanisms: bulk-forming holds water and expands stool; osmotic draws water into the lumen; stimulant activates enteric nerves; secretagogue increases chloride and fluid secretion → softer stool, faster transit.
**Loperamide — a peripheral opioid-receptor agonist that slows GI motility without significant CNS (opioid) effects at normal doses.**
Opioid brake on the gut: opioid agonist binds mu receptors on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine release → slower peristalsis, longer transit → more water absorbed, firmer stool.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — a combination opioid-receptor agonist; **atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose**.
Bismuth subsalicylate — antisecretory, mild antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory effects; also used for dyspepsia.
Opioid receptor antagonists (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine, alvimopan) block gut μ-receptors without entering the CNS, so analgesia is kept.
**PEG is first-line for chronic constipation**; magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD.

Onset (Figure 2, illustrative): osmotic ~2 h and stimulant ~8 h act fastest; secretagogue ~1 day; stool softener ~2 days and bulk-forming ~60 h take longest. **A patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming candidate.**
Stimulants cause cramping and are for short-term use. Lubiprostone causes nausea; linaclotide causes diarrhea.

t: **Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate/atropine) in suspected infectious/inflammatory diarrhea (e.g., C. difficile, invasive bacterial infection) — can worsen outcomes by delaying toxin/pathogen clearance.** Also avoid in bloody or febrile diarrhea.

Bulk-forming agents need adequate fluids and are avoided in obstruction. Linaclotide: contraindicated in mechanical obstruction and in children under 2; secretagogues avoided in mechanical obstruction.
Diphenoxylate/atropine is **Schedule V**; avoided in young children (the slides give under 2 and under 6; the profile says under 6).
Antidiarrheals should not be used with bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity.
Psyllium: separate from other drugs by 2 hours.
Bisacodyl: do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk.
Loperamide has limited CNS entry because of P-gp efflux.
Senna works in 6–12 hours orally; bisacodyl in 6–10 hours orally and 30–60 minutes rectally.
Slowing transit in an infectious or inflammatory process can worsen the picture (toxic megacolon risk in C. difficile) — “stopping diarrhea” is not always the right first move.

Case: profuse watery diarrhea and fever three days after clindamycin. **Is loperamide an appropriate choice for symptomatic relief in this patient?** No — think C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat the infection (oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin).

t: **Mesalamine, sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa.** Sulfasalazine reaches the colon → colonic bacteria cleave the azo bond → 5-ASA (mesalamine) plus sulfapyridine released → 5-ASA acts on mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators → less mucosal inflammation.
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine → metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides → block purine synthesis in lymphocytes → fewer proliferating T and B cells → slow, sustained remission.

**Targeted therapy:** TNF-α inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab); the integrin inhibitor blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing (vedolizumab); the IL-12/23 inhibitor blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling (ustekinumab); the JAK inhibitor blocks intracellular JAK signaling (tofacitinib).
Vedolizumab is the most **gut-selective** agent — less systemic immunosuppression than TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurines.
**Chemistry & formulations:** azo compounds (sulfasalazine, balsalazide, olsalazine) are cleaved by colonic bacteria; mesalamine formulations release 5-ASA at set pH or times.
5-ASA: first-line for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis; more limited role in Crohn disease.
Corticosteroids: short-term induction of remission during an acute flare; not appropriate for long-term maintenance given cumulative toxicity.
Immunomodulators: long-term maintenance of remission; onset is slow (weeks to months) — not useful for acute flares.
Delayed-release forms target the ileum or colon; enemas and suppositories treat distal disease.
Corticosteroids: prednisone 40–60 mg/d for flares, tapered after response; rectal forms for distal disease; not for maintenance.
**The major safety theme across immunomodulators and biologics: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.**

Therapy is matched to severity: mild disease responds to 5-ASA with a favorable safety profile; biologics are reserved for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease given cost, administration burden, and immunosuppression risks.

Why is vedolizumab gut-selective? α4β7 integrin is the gut-homing address tag; block it and leukocytes can’t enter the bowel, while immunity elsewhere is spared.
Why give folic acid with sulfasalazine? Sulfapyridine causes folate deficiency.
**What patients take on their own can change how their medications work.** Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels?

**Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K):** stored in adipose tissue and the liver; accumulate with excess intake — real toxicity risk; absorption depends on dietary fat and bile, impaired by fat-malabsorption conditions.
**Water-soluble (B-complex, C):** not significantly stored — excreted renally; toxicity is rare except at very high supplemental doses; deficiency develops more quickly without ongoing intake.

Figure 8 (illustrative storage/toxicity-risk index): vitamin A 85 and D 90 (fat-soluble) vs. C 10 and B-complex 8 (water-soluble). Vitamin D and A toxicity from OTC overuse are the clearest real examples.
Cyanocobalamin (B12), folic acid, vitamin D, phytonadione (K1), ferrous sulfate.

t: **B12 absorption:** dietary B12 is bound to food protein → stomach acid and pepsin release it → free B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Reduced vitamin K is recycled by VKORC1; **warfarin blocks VKORC1, so fewer active factors** — active vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors II, VII, IX, X — so fewer active factors.

**Two ways to lower warfarin’s effect:** dietary vitamin K opposes it pharmacodynamically (supports clotting factor synthesis); St. John’s wort induces CYP enzymes and speeds clearance — a pharmacokinetic interaction. **Result: lower INR and less anticoagulation.**
**Enteral nutrition** (oral or tube feeding) is preferred whenever the gut is functional — **“if the gut works, use it”**; lower infection/complication risk.

**Parenteral nutrition** is delivered intravenously, bypassing the GI tract entirely; reserved for a non-functional or inaccessible GI tract; requires close monitoring — electrolyte shifts, refeeding syndrome, catheter-related infection (the main parenteral risk).
Treat B12 deficiency with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12.
**Vitamin B12 deficiency:** megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms/neuropathy that can become irreversible if treatment is delayed.

t: St. John’s wort: avoid with SSRIs, transplant drugs, HIV protease inhibitors, oral contraceptives, warfarin.
**St. John’s Wort — CYP3A4 induction; reduces effectiveness of many drugs (warfarin, oral contraceptives, some antiretrovirals).**
**Ginkgo biloba and fish oil — can increase bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.**
**At risk for B12 deficiency:** long-term PPI or H2 blocker use, metformin (impairs ileal uptake), bariatric surgery, older age, vegan diets.
St. John’s wort activates PXR, inducing CYP 3A4, 2C9, 1A2 and P-glycoprotein: lowers digoxin, birth control, cyclosporine, HIV drugs, warfarin; serotonin syndrome with antidepressants.
Garlic, ginkgo and ginseng have antiplatelet effects — avoid or monitor with anticoagulants and around surgery.
Coenzyme Q10 and melatonin may decrease warfarin’s effect; glucosamine may increase the INR.
Fat-soluble vitamin absorption depends on dietary fat and bile.
Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users.
**Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.** Check INR when starting or stopping any supplement; stopping St. John’s wort can raise INR.
**Refeeding:** start feeding slowly in malnourished patients; check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start; give thiamine before feeding begins.
**Supplements are not held to the same FDA premarket efficacy/safety standards as prescription drugs — potency and purity can vary by product.**
Always ask patients specifically about supplement use — many don’t mention it unless asked; counsel them to disclose all supplement use to every prescriber and pharmacist.

Laxatives fall into four buckets — **bulk-forming** (slowest, safest), **osmotic** (fast; PEG first-line), **stimulant** (short-term), **secretagogue** (IBS-C) — and osmotic/stimulant act in hours, bulk-forming in days.

IBD therapy **steps up with severity**: 5-ASA → short-term steroids → thiopurines for maintenance (test TPMT/NUDT15; cut dose with allopurinol) → biologics/small molecules.

**Fat-soluble** vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate; water-soluble are excreted. Long-term **PPI or metformin** → check **B12**; refeed slowly with thiamine.

Warfarin’s effect falls with **dietary vitamin K** (pharmacodynamic) and with **St. John’s wort** (CYP3A4 induction, pharmacokinetic); ginkgo and fish oil raise bleeding — always ask about supplements.
L09 · Renal Pharmacotherapeutics — Session 1 — study guide
**Where diuretics act, and why renal function changes how every drug is dosed.** Renal physiology and pharmacokinetic principles set the dosing logic for everything that follows.
**The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.**
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.

This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit: renal dosing is not a separate topic but the lens through which every drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

Digoxin, most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session are examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment.

t: Flow (Figure 1): GFR falls → renally cleared drug or active metabolite accumulates → toxicity.

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): filtrate flows through the proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct — each diuretic class blocks sodium reabsorption at a different, specific segment.**
Share of filtered sodium reabsorbed: proximal tubule about 65%, thick ascending limb about 25%, distal tubule 5-8%, collecting duct 2-3% — this previews the potency ranking in Figure 7.
This nephron map is the conceptual spine of the session — every diuretic class is anchored back to its segment.
Match each diuretic class to the nephron segment where it acts: loop diuretics (furosemide) — thick ascending limb; thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) — distal convoluted tubule.

Potassium-sparing — aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride) — collecting duct; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) — proximal tubule; osmotic diuretics (mannitol) — throughout.
CAI — proximal tubule; osmotic — acts osmotically throughout the filtrate-containing segments, mainly the proximal tubule and descending limb.
Renal tubule transport mechanisms: the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 66% of Na⁺ and 85% of NaHCO₃; organic acid secretion there delivers most diuretics to their luminal site.
Collecting tubule system: only 2–5% of NaCl, but where aldosterone acts and K⁺ is secreted; upstream diuretics deliver more Na⁺ here — the basis of diuretic K⁺ wasting.
Renal autacoids: adenosine (A1) lowers GFR; prostaglandins (PGE2) aid loop action; natriuretic peptides (nesiritide) and urodilatin cause natriuresis but have a limited clinical role.
Three levers: reduce the dose, extend the dosing interval, or both — the specific approach depends on the drug. Reduced GFR makes a renally cleared drug accumulate if unadjusted.
Reduce the maintenance dose when the drug’s effect is concentration-dependent; extend the dosing interval when the drug has a long half-life; monitor for toxicity after each dose change.
Loading doses are often unchanged; maintenance doses are what get adjusted.
As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.

t: **Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).**
Pharmacokinetics in two numbers: volume of distribution links amount in the body to concentration; clearance links elimination rate to concentration.
Maintenance dose = clearance × target concentration (steady state depends only on clearance); loading dose = volume of distribution × target concentration, given slowly IV.
Drug accumulation: doses repeated more often than every four half-lives accumulate; steady state takes about four half-lives.
Check creatinine clearance before dosing any renally cleared drug (lower maintenance dose, extend the interval, or check CrCl) — especially in older adults.
Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration, or new nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.
When in doubt, consult dosing references or clinical pharmacy — this is not a "memorize every number" exercise; the point is the habit of checking renal function before dosing.
Distribution & clearance: adjust a renally cleared drug in proportion to creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault; women 85% of the calculated value).
The target concentration strategy: choose a target, predict V and CL from weight and renal function, dose, measure the response, revise, repeat.
Dosing history: without it a drug level loses its predictive value; draw digoxin at least 6 hours after a dose.
Renal function determines drug dosing broadly, not just for diuretics — GFR/creatinine clearance should be checked before dosing any renally cleared drug (Chapter 3).
Textbook case: 85-year-old, 60 kg, CrCl 22 mL/min — digoxin clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day: two 62.5-mcg tablets.
What changes: Dose, interval, or both — depends on the drug · Practical consideration: Estimate CrCl or eGFR before dosing, especially in older adults

g: L09 · Part 2 · Prototype + other drugs named

t: **Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.**

**Figure 3. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, reducing Na+/Cl-/K+ reabsorption and collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption —**

**explaining the increased calcium and magnesium excretion seen with this class.** The lumen-positive potential (from K⁺ recycling) is the link students skip when they memorize “loops cause hypocalcemia” without the why.
**Mechanism: block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule — a less potent natriuretic site (~5–8% of filtered sodium) than the loop.**
Follow the thiazide chain step by step (Figure 4): NCC block in the DCT → sodium and water loss → lower intracellular sodium → calcium retained through the NCX exchanger → falling urinary calcium.
Contrast this with loop diuretics, which raise urinary calcium (Figure 3).

In one line: loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption (↑ excretion); thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption through a separate mechanism (↓ excretion).
Loops work from the lumen, so their effect tracks proximal secretion; NSAIDs and probenecid compete and reduce it. NSAIDs also blunt the PGE2 contribution.
Loops: edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).
Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides.
Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone — first-line agents for essential hypertension; chlorthalidone has a longer half-life and is often preferred for 24-hour BP control.
Thiazides decrease calcium excretion — can be therapeutically useful in patients with osteoporosis and recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones.
Hypercalcemia: normal saline plus IV furosemide (80–120 mg) — a loop alone causes volume contraction and stops working.
Nephrolithiasis: thiazide plus more fluid and less salt; do not restrict dietary calcium.
Diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic, including lithium-induced): thiazides reduce polyuria; amiloride blocks lithium entry; monitor lithium levels.
Nonedematous states, hypertension: chlorthalidone lowers BP more than HCTZ but has more adverse effects; loops reserved for GFR < 30–40 mL/min or heart failure.
**Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.**

t: Furosemide carries a sulfonamide-related structure — historical cross-reactivity concern with sulfa allergy, though the clinical risk is now considered low; still worth a careful allergy history.
Thiazides lose efficacy as GFR falls below approximately 30 mL/min — loop diuretics are generally preferred once renal function is significantly reduced.

Lithium: levels rise with thiazides. NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.
Diuretic combinations: loop agents and thiazides (often metolazone) are synergistic in loop resistance — but cause large fluid shifts and K⁺ wasting.
Chlorthalidone: long half-life of 40-60 hours.

Furosemide lasts 2–3 hours; torsemide 4–6 hours and absorbs in 1 hour, nearly as completely as IV. Torsemide is mainly cleared by the liver.
Chemistry & pharmacokinetics: all thiazides are sulfonamides given orally; chlorothiazide is the only parenteral thiazide.
Loops: monitor potassium, magnesium, creatinine. Thiazides: monitor sodium, potassium, calcium, glucose.
IV furosemide slowly (no faster than 4 mg/min) — ototoxicity with rapid IV or high doses.

The calcium-handling difference between loops and thiazides is one of the highest-yield comparison points in this whole unit: loops increase Ca2+ excretion, thiazides decrease it — state it both ways.

Case: hypertension and worsening CKD (eGFR now 25 mL/min), well controlled on chlorthalidone for years, but blood pressure has crept up. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**

**Thiazide diuretics lose much of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min, because there is too little filtered sodium reaching the distal tubule for the drug to act on meaningfully.**
**A loop diuretic, which acts upstream at the thick ascending limb, remains effective even in advanced CKD and is the more appropriate choice here.**
The “thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD” point bridges directly to Session 2’s hypertension-in-CKD content.
Edematous states, heart failure: loops are standard, but overdiuresis cuts preload and cardiac output; hypokalemia worsens arrhythmias and digitalis toxicity.
Kidney disease and renal failure: little benefit below GFR 5 mL/min; high-dose loops or loop plus metolazone treat overload; avoid acetazolamide.
Textbook case: HCTZ added to chronic furosemide in CKD → 15 kg lost, BP 91/58, creatinine 10.8 — hypovolemic AKI; monitor closely, ideally inpatient.
Site, potency · Loop diuretics: Thick ascending limb — most potent natriuresis (~25%) · Thiazide diuretics: Distal convoluted tubule — modest natriuresis (~5–8%)

t: Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor → increases ENaC and Na/K pump activity → K+ and H+ secreted into the tubule. Blocking either step reduces potassium and hydrogen secretion.
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the receptor (block aldosterone’s effect directly); amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly, independent of aldosterone.
**Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor):** blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule → less HCO3- reabsorbed → bicarbonate diuresis, metabolic acidosis; weak diuretic effect.
**Mannitol (osmotic diuretic):** an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically — osmotic diuresis.
Side by side: acetazolamide removes bicarbonate reabsorption; mannitol removes water reabsorption by staying in the lumen. Both act before the loop, so their natriuretic potency is modest.
Figure 6 (**Schematic (illustrative)**): proximal tubule — carbonic anhydrase inhibition and osmotic holding of water (illustrative schematic).

**Figure 7. Original illustrative comparison (illustrative values, not from Katzung): loop diuretics block roughly 25% of filtered sodium reabsorption, substantially more than thiazides, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, or potassium-sparing diuretics —**
**directly reflecting the percentage normally reabsorbed at each nephron segment in Figure 2.** This is why loops are reached for first when potent natriuresis is the goal.
Potassium-sparing agents are often used in combination with a loop or thiazide diuretic specifically to offset potassium loss from the more potent class.
Acetazolamide: valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction; also raised intracranial pressure.
Mannitol: used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention.
Know the niche, not an everyday use: acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness; mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction.
Potassium-sparing diuretics fit mineralocorticoid excess: primary (Conn syndrome) or secondary hyperaldosteronism (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
Hepatic cirrhosis: resistant to loops but unusually responsive to spironolactone; aggressive diuresis risks hepatorenal syndrome and encephalopathy.
Renal & cardiac protection: aldosterone antagonists are cardioprotective and lower albuminuria; finerenone slowed CKD in type 2 diabetes.
Idiopathic edema (women 20–30): rule out surreptitious diuretic use; prefer moderate salt restriction.

**Primary adverse effect across the class: hyperkalemia — the risk rises sharply when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or in renal impairment (a direct preview of Session 2's cardiorenal drug-interaction content).**

Case: a patient with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and heart failure is taking an ACE inhibitor and is started on spironolactone for additional heart-failure benefit; two weeks later a routine basic metabolic panel shows potassium 6.1 mEq/L.
**What is the mechanistic explanation for this finding, and what does it suggest about future drug combinations in this unit?**

**Both the ACE inhibitor (by reducing aldosterone) and spironolactone (by directly blocking the aldosterone receptor) independently reduce potassium excretion — combined, and in the setting of CKD (which already impairs potassium excretion), the hyperkalemia risk compounds.**
**This is the same additive-risk logic that will reappear as the "triple whammy" in Session 2.** The ACEi/aldosterone-antagonist pair is one of three “whammies” formalized next session.

L10 · Renal Pharmacotherapeutics — Session 2 — study guide
**One pathway, four drug classes, and the preferred therapy for hypertension in CKD.** Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway these drugs act on.

**Figure 8. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angiotensinogen is converted to angiotensin I by renin, then to angiotensin II by ACE; angiotensin II drives both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.**
**Direct renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aldosterone antagonists each block a different point in this cascade.**
This is the conceptual spine for the session: walk the cascade before naming drugs — angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.
ACE inhibitors: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril — "-pril" suffix across the class. ARBs: losartan, valsartan — "-sartan" suffix. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren.
g: L10 · Part 1 · Prototype + other drugs named

t: **Mechanism: block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (Figure 8).**

ACE also breaks down bradykinin: ACE inhibitor blocks ACE → less angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) → less bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin accumulates → cough or angioedema → switch to an ARB for cough.
ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, rather than preventing angiotensin II formation. Aliskiren blocks the rate-limiting first step of the entire cascade.

Renoprotection: by reducing angiotensin II, these drugs preferentially dilate the efferent (outflow) arteriole of the glomerulus, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a direct, structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic BP control.

Chain (Figure 10): angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that signal → efferent arteriole dilates; intraglomerular pressure falls → proteinuria falls; creatinine rises up to ~30%.
**ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line antihypertensive therapy in CKD, especially with proteinuria — not simply because they lower blood pressure.**
ARBs: no bradykinin-related cough — preferred alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable. ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
Aliskiren: limited clinical use; useful mainly as a teaching example of where a drug could act upstream of ACE — included for conceptual completeness on Figure 8.
The drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.
**Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin accumulation — the single most common reason for switching to an ARB), angioedema (rare but potentially life-threatening), and hyperkalemia.**

Hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics rises with drugs that cut renin or angiotensin II: β blockers, NSAIDs, aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs.
Enalapril’s ACE-inhibition half-life is about 4 hours, yet once-daily dosing works: concentrations stay far above the C50, so ACE stays inhibited.
**Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks of starting or up-titrating therapy, and periodically thereafter.**
**Hold or use with caution during acute illness causing volume depletion ("sick day rules") — combined with reduced renal perfusion, RAAS blockade can precipitate acute kidney injury.**

Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration. An early creatinine rise is expected and hemodynamic, not nephrotoxicity; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

Case: a patient with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on lisinopril; two weeks later serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. **Is this an indication to stop the ACE inhibitor?**
**A rise of roughly 27% is within the expected range for ACE inhibitor initiation, reflecting reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — not drug toxicity.**
**Therapy should generally continue with ongoing monitoring; a rise beyond approximately 30%, or a much sharper increase, should prompt evaluation for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.**
A student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

**RAAS blockers are first-line — but rarely the whole story.** Other major classes: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.
This four-card slide is a brief classification recap — CCBs and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework.

Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil). Beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol. Central α2 agonists: clonidine, methyldopa. Direct arteriolar vasodilator: hydralazine.

t: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine): arteriolar dilation. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil): also ↓ HR/contractility.
Beta-blockers: ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin release.
Chain (Figure 11): dihydropyridine arteriolar dilation → afterload falls; blood pressure lowers. Non-DHP CCB or beta-blocker: heart rate and contractility fall → renin release falls.
Clonidine or methyldopa stimulates central α2 receptors → sympathetic outflow falls, so BP falls. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Beta-blockers: not generally first-line for uncomplicated HTN, but compelling indications include concurrent CAD/heart failure/arrhythmia.

If all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD? Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection — the renoprotective gap in Figure 12, not a difference in BP control.
Thiazide / loop diuretics (covered in depth in Session 1): thiazides first-line with preserved renal function; loops preferred as GFR falls.
Central agents (clonidine, methyldopa) and hydralazine: reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations (e.g., methyldopa in pregnancy).
Diuretics enhance the efficacy of many agents, particularly ACE inhibitors; hydralazine and minoxidil need a diuretic because they cause salt and water retention.
Spironolactone may be the most effective single agent for drug-resistant hypertension.
Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect.

**Resistant hypertension (BP above goal despite three or more antihypertensive classes, including a diuretic) is common in CKD, often driven by volume overload.**
First step: confirm diuretic therapy is adequate — a thiazide may simply no longer be effective at the patient’s current GFR (Session 1’s loop-vs-thiazide cutoff).
Switching from a thiazide to a loop diuretic, or increasing loop diuretic dosing, is often the most effective single change in advanced CKD.
**Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can be added for resistant hypertension, but require close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB.**

"Resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class — check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

Case: CKD (eGFR 28 mL/min), still hypertensive despite lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. **What is the most likely contributor to inadequate control, and what change would you suggest first?**

**At this GFR, hydrochlorothiazide has largely lost its natriuretic efficacy (Session 1). Switching to a loop diuretic such as furosemide or torsemide is usually the most effective next step before adding an entirely new drug class.**

**Where cardiovascular and renal pharmacology converge — and where that convergence can go wrong.** This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angina results when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply; nitrates reduce preload, dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload,**
**non-dihydropyridine CCBs also reduce heart rate/contractility and increase coronary flow, and beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility.**
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto it from memory.
Nitroglycerin (sublingual for acute angina; IV/patch for sustained use), isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate (oral, longer-acting).

t: **Mechanism: release nitric oxide, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP, producing smooth muscle relaxation — predominantly venodilation at usual doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.**
Chain (Figure 14): nitrate donates nitric oxide (NO) → NO activates guanylate cyclase, so cGMP rises → cGMP relaxes smooth muscle: venodilation → preload and oxygen demand fall.
**Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — predominantly arteriolar dilation, reducing afterload; the same mechanism used for hypertension (Section 5).**

**Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — also reduce heart rate and contractility and increase coronary blood flow; avoid combining with beta-blockers due to additive bradycardia/AV block risk.**
CCBs are the clearest example in the unit of the same drug class, same mechanism, treating two different conditions (hypertension and angina).

This is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5; they are the same drugs doing double duty.
**Adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.**

t: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and similar) — the combination can cause life-threatening hypotension.**
PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil block cGMP breakdown, causing severe hypotension with nitrates.
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question worth a memorable callout.

**Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): an NSAID (afferent arteriolar constriction), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent arteriolar dilation), and a diuretic (volume depletion) each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure —**
**combined, the effect on kidney perfusion is additive to synergistic, substantially raising acute kidney injury risk.** An extremely common, often missed, entirely preventable cause of AKI.
Three hits (Figure 17): NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent arteriole → diuretic causes volume depletion → filtration pressure collapses: AKI.
NSAIDs blunt loop and thiazide action by reducing renal prostaglandins — significant in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis.
Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.
Prevention: counsel patients about over-the-counter NSAIDs — ask which OTC NSAIDs they commonly take.
The triple whammy is the capstone cardiorenal interaction: Session 1’s diuretics + this session’s RAAS blockers + NSAIDs students will meet constantly in practice.
Hypertension → CKD: uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular capillary injury and nephrosclerosis over time — a leading cause of CKD progression, alongside diabetes.
CKD → hypertension: reduced renal function causes volume overload and RAAS activation, which worsens and complicates blood pressure control, often requiring multiple drug classes.

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hypertension and chronic kidney disease drive one another in a self-reinforcing cycle — uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular injury and CKD progression,**
**while CKD causes volume overload and RAAS activation that worsens hypertension.**
Figure 18 is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Case: an older adult on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts a regular OTC NSAID for a knee injury; one week later, lethargy and an acute rise in creatinine. **What is the most likely explanation, and how could this have been prevented?**

**This is a classic "triple whammy" presentation (Figure 16) — the NSAID, ACE inhibitor, and diuretic each independently reduced glomerular filtration pressure, and together precipitated acute kidney injury.**
**Prevention requires counseling patients on RAAS blockers and diuretics to avoid regular NSAID use and to seek guidance before starting one, even an over-the-counter product.**
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling): the preventable element is entirely what the patient was or wasn’t told about OTC NSAID use.

Same patient, eGFR now 25: hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is more effective for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue.
Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

t: Stems: **-pril**, **-sartan**, **-kiren**, **-dipine**, **-olol**, **-azine / -alazine**, **-onidine**, **-nitrate / nitro-**, **-afil**, **-semide**. Read the **Stem**, name the **Class**, recall the **Examples** and the **Memory aid**.
Why are nitrates + sildenafil deadly? Nitrates make cGMP; sildenafil stops its breakdown — cGMP piles up and blood pressure collapses.

**Applying the whole Renal pharmacology toolkit.** Integration: put the drug classes together — for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

**1.** Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
**2.** ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
**3.** Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
**4.** The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
**5.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
All three threads center on glomerular filtration pressure.

Connecting back to earlier units: drug-metabolism/dosing concepts (Unit 1) and the biologic-mechanism callbacks from Units 2–4 all reinforce that pharmacology is cumulative — the cardiorenal interface is where several organ-system units visibly intersect.
**Patient A — advancing CKD, hypertension no longer controlled on a thiazide:** switch to a loop diuretic; check potassium and volume status.
**Patient B — proteinuric CKD, needs first-line antihypertensive therapy:** ACE inhibitor or ARB; check potassium and creatinine in 1–2 weeks and pregnancy potential.
**Patient C — on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, about to start a daily OTC NSAID:** counsel against regular NSAID use — triple whammy AKI risk.

**Patient D — stable angina, already on a beta-blocker, needs additional symptom control:** add a dihydropyridine CCB or a long-acting nitrate; avoid diltiazem/verapamil (AV block) and PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.

t: Every case, two answers: **the approach** and **the one thing to check**.
RAAS blocks — Aliskiren renin · -pril ACE · -sartan AT1 · spironolactone aldosterone
ACEi adverse effects — Cough (bradykinin), angioedema, hyperkalemia
ACEi cough → ? — Switch to an ARB
ACEi/ARB in pregnancy — Contraindicated (fetal renal toxicity)
Why first-line in proteinuric CKD — Efferent dilation → ↓ intraglomerular pressure, ↓ proteinuria
Creatinine after ACEi — Up to ~30% expected; more → stenosis or volume depletion
Monitoring — K⁺ and creatinine within 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules
Aliskiren — Never with ACEi/ARB in diabetes
DHP vs. non-DHP — Arterioles · heart rate/contractility
Non-DHP + beta-blocker — Bradycardia, AV block
Hydralazine — Pair with beta-blocker + diuretic
Clonidine — Rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly
Methyldopa — Hypertension in pregnancy
Nitrates — NO → cGMP → venodilation; nitrate-free interval
Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor — Absolute contraindication — hypotension
HTN and angina, one mechanism — Calcium channel blockers
Triple whammy — NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic
Once-daily ACE inhibitor — Levels stay far above C50
Hydralazine + diuretic — Vasodilators cause salt and water retention

The **RAAS**: angiotensinogen → (renin) → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone; aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aldosterone antagonists each block one step.

**ACE inhibitors/ARBs** are first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure; a creatinine rise **up to ~30%** is expected; check K⁺/creatinine in 1–2 weeks; **never in pregnancy**.

t: ACE-inhibitor **cough** is bradykinin, not allergy → switch to an **ARB**; angioedema → stop.
**Non-DHP CCBs + beta-blockers** → bradycardia/AV block; resistant HTN in CKD is often a thiazide that needs to become a **loop**.
**Nitrates**: NO → cGMP → venodilation; nitrate-free interval; **never with PDE5 inhibitors**. **CCBs** treat both hypertension and angina by the same mechanism.
**Triple whammy**: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI; counsel against OTC NSAIDs.

t: Acetaminophen — Analgesic and antipyretic (not an NSAID)
Acetaminophen: Analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central (reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; hypothalamic temperature center); minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action.
Acetaminophen: Textbook: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor; pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.
Acetaminophen: Mild-to-moderate pain and fever; reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Acetaminophen: Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for RA.
Acetaminophen: Caution in liver disease, significant alcohol use, or malnutrition (prolonged fasting, anorexia).
Acetaminophen: Overdose: glutathione depleted → NAPQI accumulates → binds hepatocyte proteins → centrilobular liver necrosis.
Acetaminophen: Ingesting 15 g may be fatal; even 4 g/day is associated with liver function test abnormalities.
Acetaminophen: Combination cold, flu, and sleep products hide acetaminophen — unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of liver injury. Ask about ALL sources.
Acetaminophen: Combined with an NSAID it improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.
Acetaminophen: Chronic alcohol use and fasting lower glutathione and induce CYP2E1 → higher toxicity risk.
Acetaminophen: Safer first-line than an NSAID when NSAID red flags (CKD, anticoagulant, older age) stack up.
Acetaminophen: Generic name — sold as Tylenol and many store brands; two brands can hide the same ingredient.
Acetaminophen: Metabolism: ~90% glucuronidation/sulfation (safe); ~5–10% CYP2E1 → NAPQI, neutralized by glutathione at therapeutic doses.

Acetaminophen: Acute single ingestion: plot a 4-hour-or-later level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram — above the line, give N-acetylcysteine (early); check AST/ALT. Not used after 24 h or for chronic ingestion.
Acetaminophen: Normal Phase I metabolism makes the toxic metabolite NAPQI (Lecture 1’s example).
Acetaminophen: Adults generally no more than 4 g/day; half-life 2–3 h; N-acetylcysteine within 8–16 hours prevents fulminant hepatotoxicity.
Albuterol — Selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist
Albuterol: Binds and activates β2 → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.
Albuterol: The lecture’s model for receptor-to-response logic you reuse for every agonist.
Warfarin — Anticoagulant
Warfarin: NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
Warfarin: Inducers (barbiturates, St. John’s wort) lower its level; stopping the inducer raises it and can cause bleeding.
Warfarin: Celecoxib (CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts; tocilizumab stimulates CYP450, so warfarin doses may need adjusting.
Warfarin: Dose requirements vary up to 20-fold; CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes explain much of it.
Warfarin: Classic narrow-therapeutic-index drug — careful dosing and blood-level monitoring.
Warfarin: 99% protein-bound; half-life about 37 h.
Warfarin: Venous thromboembolism, atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves
Warfarin: Bleeding, bruising, hair loss, skin necrosis (rare)
Warfarin: Pregnancy (most cases), active bleeding, recent CNS surgery, uncontrolled hypertension
Warfarin: Toxicity/overdose: Hemorrhage; reversal with vitamin K and 4-factor PCC; many interactions (St. John's wort lowers INR)
Warfarin: Formulation: Tablet 1/2/2.5/3/4/5/6/7.5/10 mg. Adult dose: Start 2-5 mg PO daily, adjust to INR goal (usually 2-3).
Lithium
Lithium: Celecoxib raises lithium levels.
Lithium: Thiazides raise lithium levels — monitor.
Lithium: Renally cleared with a narrow TI — adjust dose or interval in renal impairment.
Lithium: Classic narrow-TI drug requiring blood-level monitoring.
Lithium: About 95% excreted unchanged in urine, 0% protein-bound; target ~0.7 mEq/L, toxic above 2 mEq/L; half-life ~22 h.
Digoxin
Digoxin: Inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) raises digoxin blood levels.
Digoxin: Hypokalemia from loop diuretics increases digoxin toxicity.
Digoxin: Renally cleared — adjust dose or interval in renal impairment.
Digoxin: Older adult with CrCl 22 mL/min: clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day (two 62.5-mcg tablets); draw levels at least 6 hours after a dose.
Digoxin: Classic narrow-TI drug requiring blood-level monitoring.
Digoxin: Very high Vd — mostly sequestered in tissue, not plasma.
Digoxin: Vd ~500 L, half-life ~39 h; target ~1 ng/mL, toxic above 2 ng/mL.
Phenytoin
Phenytoin: A CYP inducer — lowers levels of CYP substrates.
Phenytoin: Classic narrow-TI drug requiring blood-level monitoring.
Phenytoin: Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination — clearance falls as concentration rises.
Phenytoin: Target ~10 mg/L, toxic above 20 mg/L; 89% protein-bound.
Nitroglycerin — Organic nitrate
Nitroglycerin: Large first-pass effect — needs a higher oral dose or a non-oral route; sublingual dosing enters systemic veins directly, bypassing the liver.
Nitroglycerin: Releases nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venodilation → ↓ preload and O₂ demand.
Nitroglycerin: Acute angina, angina prophylaxis, acute heart failure, hypertensive emergency
Nitroglycerin: Headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness
Nitroglycerin: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) or riociguat, severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure, right ventricular infarction
Nitroglycerin: Toxicity/overdose: Severe hypotension and syncope, especially with PDE5 inhibitors; tolerance without a nitrate-free interval; methemoglobinemia at very high doses

Nitroglycerin: Formulation: Sublingual tablet 0.3/0.4/0.6 mg; spray 0.4 mg; patch 0.1-0.8 mg/h; IV infusion. Adult dose: Acute angina: 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes up to 3 doses; patch 0.2-0.8 mg/h applied 12-14 hours per day; IV 5-10 mcg/min titrated.
Nitroglycerin: Acute angina: 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes up to 3 doses.
Nitroglycerin: Absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — life-threatening hypotension; nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.
Nitroglycerin: PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat → severe hypotension.
Propranolol — Nonselective β-adrenoceptor antagonist (β blocker)
Propranolol: Competitive β antagonist: exercise or stress catecholamines can overcome a fixed dose.
Propranolol: Asthma: blocking β2 can cause bronchoconstriction — a β1-selective blocker is an alternative.
Propranolol: Bronchoconstriction in asthma (β2 blockade).
Propranolol: Large first-pass effect — much higher oral than IV dose for the same exposure.
Propranolol: Slows heart rate markedly in pheochromocytoma but not a trained runner’s resting rate.
Metoprolol — β1-selective adrenoceptor antagonist
Metoprolol: Binds preferentially to β1 (heart), with lower affinity for β2.
Metoprolol: An alternative to propranolol in a patient with asthma.
Metoprolol: Beta-1 selective blocker: ↓ heart rate, contractility and renin release.
Metoprolol: Hypertension with CAD or HF, angina, post-MI, atrial fibrillation
Metoprolol: Fatigue, bradycardia, dizziness, cold extremities, sexual dysfunction, bronchospasm at high dose
Metoprolol: Severe bradycardia, high-grade AV block, decompensated HF, cardiogenic shock; do not stop abruptly
Metoprolol: Toxicity/overdose: Bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, bronchospasm; rebound tachycardia with abrupt withdrawal

Metoprolol: Formulation: Tartrate tablets 25/50/100 mg; succinate ER tablets 25-200 mg; IV injection. Adult dose: Hypertension: tartrate 50 mg PO BID or succinate 50-100 mg daily (maximum 400 mg/day); heart failure: succinate 12.5-25 mg daily, titrate.
Metoprolol: Not first-line for uncomplicated HTN; compelling with CAD, heart failure, arrhythmia; never with diltiazem/verapamil; do not stop abruptly.
Metoprolol: With diltiazem or verapamil → bradycardia, AV block.
Morphine — Opioid analgesic
Morphine: Large first-pass effect.
Morphine: Active metabolite of codeine, about 200× more potent than codeine.
Codeine — Opioid (prodrug)
Codeine: Prodrug: CYP2D6 converts it to morphine.
Codeine: CYP2D6 poor metabolizers get little relief; ultrarapid metabolizers risk toxicity — CPIC recommends an alternative analgesic for both.
Clopidogrel — Antiplatelet (prodrug)
Clopidogrel: Prodrug: about 85% of a dose is inactivated by esterases; CYP2C19 forms the active metabolite.
Clopidogrel: CYP2C19 variation affects activation; poor/intermediate metabolizers after PCI → prasugrel or ticagrelor (CPIC).
Azathioprine — Thiopurine immunosuppressant · conventional DMARD
Azathioprine: Converted to 6-mercaptopurine and then 6-thioguanine, which suppresses B- and T-cell function, immunoglobulin production, and IL-2.
Azathioprine: Active rheumatoid arthritis (2 mg/kg/day orally); prevents kidney transplant rejection.
Azathioprine: Bone marrow suppression, GI disturbance, carcinogenicity, increased infection risk.
Azathioprine: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) raises levels — reduce the dose (textbook: by 75%).
Azathioprine: TPMT deficiency raises thiopurine toxicity risk.
Azathioprine: TPMT intermediate activity: start at 30–70% of the target dose; deficient: drastically reduce or use an alternative. NUDT15 variants also predict leukopenia.
Azathioprine: Maintenance of remission in Crohn disease and UC (off-label), organ transplant
Azathioprine: Nausea, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, infection
Azathioprine: Hypersensitivity; prior alkylating therapy; use with febuxostat
Azathioprine: Toxicity/overdose: Myelosuppression (higher with low TPMT), lymphoma and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma; allopurinol requires major dose cut
Azathioprine: Formulation: Tablet 50/75/100 mg; IV. Adult dose: IBD maintenance: 1.5-2.5 mg/kg PO daily after TPMT/NUDT15 testing; onset 8-12 weeks.
Allopurinol — Xanthine oxidase inhibitor (urate-lowering therapy)
Allopurinol: Purine analog; it and its metabolite oxypurinol block xanthine oxidase → ↓ uric acid production.
Allopurinol: First-line chronic urate-lowering therapy for most patients with gout — started only after the flare resolves.
Allopurinol: Never start (or change) during an acute flare — it can prolong the flare.
Allopurinol: HLA-B*5801-positive patients: don’t use (screen Han Chinese, Korean, and Thai patients).
Allopurinol: Severe hypersensitivity / cutaneous reactions (HLA-B*58:01); can precipitate flares when starting.
Allopurinol: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (SJS/TEN, fever, eosinophilia, hepatitis, renal failure) 2–4 weeks in — stop at the first rash; pruritic rash in 3%.
Allopurinol: Reduce dose with azathioprine or mercaptopurine (textbook: cut azathioprine by 75%).
Allopurinol: Also inhibits metabolism of probenecid and oral anticoagulants; diuretics, amoxicillin, ampicillin raise hypersensitivity risk.
Allopurinol: HLA-B*5801 carriers have a sharply higher risk of severe hypersensitivity — screen before starting.
Allopurinol: Reduce the dose in renal impairment (textbook: start ≤50 mg/d in CKD).
Allopurinol: Start low (100 mg/d) and titrate toward a serum urate target (<6 mg/dL); cover with colchicine or an NSAID for 3–6 months.
Allopurinol: Don’t stop it if a flare occurs while already on it.
Allopurinol: Suggested alternative when rasburicase is contraindicated (G6PD deficiency).
Abacavir
Abacavir: HLA-B*57:01-positive patients (hypersensitivity).
Rasburicase — Uricase (recombinant enzyme)
Rasburicase: Uricase converts uric acid to allantoin, which is soluble and excreted.
Rasburicase: Uricases are reserved for refractory gout.
Rasburicase: G6PD deficiency (hemolysis) — use an alternative such as allopurinol.
Rasburicase: -ase stem = enzyme (uricase).
Aspirin — Salicylate NSAID (irreversible COX inhibitor)
Aspirin: Irreversibly acetylates platelet COX — the antiplatelet effect lasts 8–10 days (the platelet’s life).
Aspirin: Now used mainly as an antiplatelet (81–325 mg daily); low-dose aspirin also helps prevent preterm preeclampsia.
Aspirin: Hemophilia (antiplatelet action).
Aspirin: At antithrombotic doses: gastric upset and gastric/duodenal ulcers.
Aspirin: Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks its irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting cardioprotection.
Aspirin: Unlike acetaminophen, aspirin antagonizes uricosuric agents.
Aspirin: Long-term low-dose aspirin in type 2 diabetes increases GI bleeding risk.
Aspirin: Overdose: alkalinizing the urine traps ionized drug and speeds renal clearance (weak acid).
Aspirin: Hydrolyzed rapidly (serum half-life 15 minutes) to salicylate; capacity-limited (saturable) elimination.
Heparin — Anticoagulant
Heparin: Reversed by protamine, which binds it directly (chemical antagonism).
Heparin: Commonly given subcutaneously (slower, steady absorption).
Protamine — Heparin reversal agent
Protamine: Positively charged protein that binds negatively charged heparin — chemical antagonism, no receptor involved.
Protamine: Reversal of heparin.
Insulin
Insulin: Commonly given subcutaneously (slower, steady absorption).
Theophylline
Theophylline: Loading dose example: Vd 35 L × target 10 mg/L = 350 mg for a 70-kg adult.
Phenoxybenzamine — Irreversible α-adrenoceptor antagonist
Phenoxybenzamine: Irreversible α blockade that lasts until new receptors are made.
Phenoxybenzamine: Hypertension of pheochromocytoma.
Rifampin — CYP inducer
Rifampin: Induces CYP enzymes, speeding metabolism of substrates (levels fall).
St. John's wort — Herbal product · CYP3A4 inducer
