Ondansetron: Formulation: Tablet 4/8 mg; ODT 4/8 mg; oral film; IV/IM 2 mg/mL. Adult dose: 4-8 mg PO/ODT every 8 hours; IV 4 mg; chemotherapy regimens use 8-24 mg pre-dose; single IV dose max 16 mg.
Ondansetron: Give before chemotherapy; QT prolongation; CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less well.
Metoclopramide — Dopamine D2 antagonist, prokinetic
Metoclopramide: D2 antagonism in the CTZ (antiemetic) plus D2 blockade and 5-HT4 agonism in the gut → more acetylcholine → faster gastric emptying (prokinetic).
Metoclopramide: Diabetic gastroparesis, GERD (short-term), chemotherapy and postoperative nausea
Metoclopramide: Drowsiness, restlessness, diarrhea; depression
Metoclopramide: GI obstruction, perforation or bleeding; pheochromocytoma; seizure disorder; history of tardive dyskinesia
Metoclopramide: Toxicity/overdose: Boxed warning: tardive dyskinesia (may be irreversible); acute dystonia (diphenhydramine or benztropine); neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Metoclopramide: Formulation: Tablet 5/10 mg; ODT; oral solution; IV/IM 5 mg/mL. Adult dose: Gastroparesis: 10 mg PO 30 min before meals and at bedtime (max 40 mg/day); limit to 12 weeks; lower dose in renal impairment.

Metoclopramide: Boxed warning: tardive dyskinesia — avoid beyond 12 weeks; acute dystonia → diphenhydramine or benztropine; avoid in Parkinson disease; renal dosing; CYP2D6 poor metabolizers need lower doses.
Aprepitant — NK1 receptor antagonist
Aprepitant: Blocks substance P/neurokinin at NK1 receptors in the CTZ.
Aprepitant: Prevention of chemotherapy and postoperative nausea and vomiting
Aprepitant: Fatigue, constipation, hiccups, raised liver enzymes
Aprepitant: Pimozide co-use; hypersensitivity
Aprepitant: Toxicity/overdose: CYP3A4 substrate and moderate inhibitor: lowers warfarin and hormonal contraceptive effect; overdose drowsiness, headache
Aprepitant: Formulation: Capsule 40/80/125 mg; IV fosaprepitant 150 mg. Adult dose: CINV: 125 mg PO day 1, then 80 mg days 2-3, with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone; PONV: 40 mg pre-op.
Meclizine — H1 antihistamine, anticholinergic
Meclizine: Blocks histamine H1 (and acetylcholine) signals from the vestibular system.
Meclizine: Motion sickness, vertigo
Meclizine: Drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention
Meclizine: Hypersensitivity; caution in glaucoma, BPH, asthma, older adults
Meclizine: Toxicity/overdose: Anticholinergic toxicity: agitation, hallucinations, tachycardia, seizures; additive sedation
Meclizine: Formulation: Tablet 12.5/25/50 mg; chewable tablet. Adult dose: Motion sickness: 25-50 mg 1 hour before travel, repeat every 24 hours; vertigo: 25-100 mg/day divided.
Meclizine: Motion sickness is vestibular — H1/M1 blockers fit.
Scopolamine — Muscarinic antagonist
Scopolamine: Muscarinic antagonist: blocks acetylcholine from the vestibular system.
Scopolamine: Motion sickness, postoperative nausea
Scopolamine: Dry mouth, drowsiness, blurred vision, dizziness
Scopolamine: Narrow-angle glaucoma; hypersensitivity
Scopolamine: Toxicity/overdose: Anticholinergic toxicity; withdrawal nausea and dizziness; wash hands to avoid dilated pupils
Scopolamine: Formulation: Transdermal patch 1.5 mg (about 1 mg over 3 days). Adult dose: 1 patch behind the ear at least 4 hours before travel; replace every 72 hours.
Prochlorperazine — Phenothiazine D2 antagonist
Prochlorperazine: Phenothiazine: blocks dopamine D2 at the CTZ (and other receptors).
Prochlorperazine: Severe nausea and vomiting, psychosis
Prochlorperazine: Sedation, hypotension, dry mouth, extrapyramidal symptoms
Prochlorperazine: Children under 2 years, coma, dementia-related psychosis (boxed warning)
Prochlorperazine: Toxicity/overdose: Acute dystonia, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT prolongation, sedation
Prochlorperazine: Formulation: Tablet 5/10 mg; suppository 25 mg; IV/IM 5 mg/mL. Adult dose: 5-10 mg PO every 6-8 hours (max 40 mg/day); 25 mg PR every 12 hours; 5-10 mg IV/IM.
Dronabinol — Cannabinoids
Dronabinol: Synthetic cannabinoid: activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center and CTZ, reducing neurotransmitter release; also stimulates appetite — a pathway distinct from 5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1.
Dronabinol: Refractory chemotherapy nausea; anorexia in AIDS (dronabinol)
Dronabinol: Dizziness, euphoria, drowsiness, tachycardia
Dronabinol: Hypersensitivity; sesame oil allergy (dronabinol capsule)
Dronabinol: Toxicity/overdose: Psychoactive: anxiety, paranoia, tachycardia, hypotension; additive CNS depression; misuse potential

Dronabinol: Formulation: Dronabinol capsule 2.5/5/10 mg, solution; nabilone capsule 1 mg. Adult dose: Dronabinol 5 mg/m2 1-3 hours before chemotherapy, then every 2-4 hours; appetite: 2.5 mg BID; nabilone 1-2 mg BID.
Dronabinol: Reserved for refractory CINV; dronabinol Schedule III, nabilone Schedule II; caution in older adults.
Dexamethasone — Corticosteroid
Dexamethasone: Corticosteroid that adds to other antiemetics in chemotherapy regimens.
Dexamethasone: Antiemetic adjunct in chemotherapy; inflammation and allergy
Dexamethasone: Insomnia, hyperglycemia, mood change, fluid retention
Dexamethasone: Systemic fungal infection; hypersensitivity
Dexamethasone: Toxicity/overdose: Adrenal suppression with prolonged use; infection, hyperglycemia, psychosis; taper after long courses
Dexamethasone: Formulation: Tablet 0.5-6 mg; oral solution; IV 4 mg/mL. Adult dose: CINV: 8-12 mg PO/IV on day 1, then 8 mg daily on days 2-4 depending on regimen.
Polyethylene glycol 3350 — Osmotic laxative
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Osmotic laxative: draws water into the lumen.
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Chronic and occasional constipation; bowel preparation (higher volumes)
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Bloating, nausea, gas, loose stools
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Bowel obstruction, perforation, ileus, toxic megacolon
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Toxicity/overdose: Dehydration and electrolyte loss with excess or bowel-prep volumes; rare allergic reactions
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Formulation: Powder for solution (17 g scoop); large-volume bowel-prep kits. Adult dose: 17 g in 4-8 oz fluid PO once daily; OTC use up to 7 days.
Polyethylene glycol 3350: First-line for chronic constipation; fast, reliable onset.
Psyllium — Bulk-forming laxative
Psyllium: Bulk-forming laxative: absorbs water, increases stool bulk and transit.
Psyllium: Constipation, IBS, mild cholesterol lowering
Psyllium: Bloating, gas, abdominal fullness
Psyllium: Bowel obstruction, fecal impaction, dysphagia
Psyllium: Toxicity/overdose: Esophageal or intestinal obstruction if taken with too little fluid; allergy; separate from other drugs by 2 hours
Psyllium: Formulation: Powder, capsules, wafers. Adult dose: About 3.4-6 g PO 1-3 times daily with at least 8 oz water.
Psyllium: Slowest onset, safest long term; needs adequate fluids; avoid in obstruction.
Methylcellulose — Bulk-forming laxative
Methylcellulose: Bulk-forming laxative: holds water and expands stool.
Methylcellulose: Constipation, stool bulking
Methylcellulose: Bloating, gas
Methylcellulose: Bowel obstruction, dysphagia
Methylcellulose: Toxicity/overdose: Obstruction if taken without adequate fluid; may slow absorption of other drugs
Methylcellulose: Formulation: Powder; caplets 500 mg. Adult dose: About 2 g PO in 8 oz water 1-3 times daily; onset 12-72 hours.
Lactulose — Osmotic laxative, ammonia-lowering agent
Lactulose: Osmotic laxative (nonabsorbable sugar): draws water into the lumen; also lowers ammonia.
Lactulose: Constipation, hepatic encephalopathy
Lactulose: Gas, bloating, cramps, diarrhea
Lactulose: Galactosemia, bowel obstruction
Lactulose: Toxicity/overdose: Dehydration and hypernatremia with over-use; worsens diabetes control slightly
Lactulose: Formulation: Oral solution 10 g/15 mL. Adult dose: Constipation: 15-30 mL PO daily; hepatic encephalopathy: 30-45 mL PO 3-4 times daily, titrated to 2-3 soft stools.
Senna — Stimulant laxative
Senna: Stimulant laxative: directly stimulates enteric nerves and motility.
Senna: Short-term constipation, opioid-induced constipation
Senna: Cramping, diarrhea, urine discoloration, melanosis coli
Senna: Bowel obstruction, appendicitis, undiagnosed abdominal pain
Senna: Toxicity/overdose: Hypokalemia and dehydration with chronic use; laxative dependence
Senna: Formulation: Tablet 8.6 mg sennosides; liquid. Adult dose: 8.6-17.2 mg PO at bedtime (max 34 mg/day); onset 6-12 hours.
Senna: Short-term or breakthrough use; cramping.
Bisacodyl — Stimulant laxative
Bisacodyl: Stimulant laxative: activates enteric nerves.
Bisacodyl: Constipation, bowel preparation
Bisacodyl: Cramping, nausea, rectal irritation
Bisacodyl: Bowel obstruction, appendicitis, acute abdomen
Bisacodyl: Toxicity/overdose: Do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk; excess causes diarrhea, hypokalemia
Bisacodyl: Formulation: DR tablet 5 mg; suppository 10 mg. Adult dose: 5-15 mg PO at bedtime; 10 mg PR once daily; PO onset 6-12 hours, PR 15-60 min.
Lubiprostone — Chloride channel (ClC-2) activator
Lubiprostone: Secretagogue: activates the ClC-2 chloride channel → more chloride and fluid secretion.
Lubiprostone: Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C, opioid-induced constipation
Lubiprostone: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, abdominal pain
Lubiprostone: Mechanical GI obstruction
Lubiprostone: Toxicity/overdose: Dizziness, syncope or dyspnea (rare); overdose: nausea, diarrhea; avoid in pregnancy unless needed
Lubiprostone: Formulation: Capsule 8/24 mcg. Adult dose: Chronic constipation: 24 mcg PO BID with food; IBS-C (women): 8 mcg BID.
Lubiprostone: Nausea is the classic adverse effect.
Linaclotide — Guanylate cyclase-C agonist
Linaclotide: Secretagogue: guanylate cyclase-C agonist → more chloride and fluid secretion.
Linaclotide: Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C
Linaclotide: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, gas, bloating
Linaclotide: Boxed: children under 2 years; mechanical GI obstruction
Linaclotide: Toxicity/overdose: Severe dehydration (deaths in young children); severe diarrhea; stop if severe or prolonged
Linaclotide: Formulation: Capsule 72/145/290 mcg. Adult dose: CIC: 72-145 mcg PO daily; IBS-C: 290 mcg daily; 30 minutes before the first meal.
Linaclotide: Diarrhea; contraindicated in mechanical obstruction and in children under 2.
Loperamide — Peripheral mu-opioid agonist
Loperamide: Peripheral mu-opioid agonist on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine → slower peristalsis, more water absorbed; enters the CNS poorly (P-gp efflux).
Loperamide: Acute and chronic diarrhea, traveler's diarrhea
Loperamide: Constipation, cramps, dizziness, nausea
Loperamide: Bloody stool or high fever, C. difficile, children under 2, ileus
Loperamide: Toxicity/overdose: High doses: QT prolongation, torsades, cardiac arrest; CNS depression in overdose (naloxone, repeated)
Loperamide: Formulation: Capsule 2 mg; tablet 2 mg; oral liquid. Adult dose: 4 mg PO first dose, then 2 mg after each loose stool; max 16 mg/day Rx, 8 mg/day OTC.
Loperamide: Avoid in suspected C. difficile and in bloody or febrile diarrhea; very high doses → QT prolongation.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — Opioid antidiarrheal (C-V) plus anticholinergic
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Opioid-receptor agonist slows motility; atropine at a subtherapeutic dose discourages misuse.
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Adjunct for diarrhea
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Drowsiness, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Children under 6 years, obstructive jaundice, C. difficile or infectious diarrhea
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Toxicity/overdose: Respiratory depression (especially children) and anticholinergic toxicity; naloxone, with monitoring for relapse
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Formulation: Tablet 2.5 mg/0.025 mg; oral liquid 2.5 mg/5 mL. Adult dose: 5 mg (2 tablets) PO QID initially; max 20 mg/day; reduce as controlled.
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Schedule V; avoid in young children and in infectious diarrhea.
Mesalamine — 5-ASA aminosalicylate
Mesalamine: 5-ASA: anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators.
Mesalamine: Induction and maintenance in ulcerative colitis; mild Crohn disease (some forms)
Mesalamine: Headache, nausea, abdominal pain, flatulence
Mesalamine: Salicylate hypersensitivity
Mesalamine: Toxicity/overdose: Interstitial nephritis (monitor creatinine); acute intolerance syndrome (cramps, bloody diarrhea); hepatotoxicity rare

Mesalamine: Formulation: DR tablet 800 mg/1.2 g; capsule; suppository 1,000 mg; enema 4 g/60 mL. Adult dose: Mild-moderate UC: 2.4-4.8 g/day PO once daily or divided; 1,000 mg PR at bedtime for proctitis.
Mesalamine: First-line for mild-to-moderate UC; monitor renal function (interstitial nephritis); enemas/suppositories for distal disease.
Budesonide — Locally acting corticosteroid
Budesonide: Locally acting corticosteroid with high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone.
Budesonide: Mild-moderate ileocecal Crohn disease, mild-moderate UC
Budesonide: Headache, nausea, acne, adrenal suppression with long courses
Budesonide: Hypersensitivity
Budesonide: Toxicity/overdose: Hypercortisolism with CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, grapefruit juice); infection risk
Budesonide: Formulation: Capsule 3 mg; ER tablet 9 mg; foam. Adult dose: Crohn disease: 9 mg PO every morning for up to 8 weeks; UC: 9 mg ER tablet daily for 8 weeks.
Budesonide: Short-term induction of remission; not for maintenance.
Mercaptopurine — Purine antimetabolite
Mercaptopurine: Thiopurine: metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides that block purine synthesis in lymphocytes.
Mercaptopurine: Maintenance in Crohn disease and UC; acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Mercaptopurine: Nausea, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis
Mercaptopurine: Hypersensitivity; use with febuxostat
Mercaptopurine: Toxicity/overdose: Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, lymphoma risk; reduce dose with allopurinol
Mercaptopurine: Formulation: Tablet 50 mg; oral suspension. Adult dose: IBD (off-label): 1-1.5 mg/kg PO daily after TPMT/NUDT15 testing.
Mercaptopurine: Test TPMT and NUDT15 first; allopurinol → cut dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters; monitor CBC and LFTs; onset weeks to months.
Vedolizumab — Humanized alpha4beta7 integrin antibody
Vedolizumab: Blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing — gut-selective, less systemic immunosuppression.
Vedolizumab: Moderate-severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease
Vedolizumab: Nasopharyngitis, headache, arthralgia, infusion reactions
Vedolizumab: Hypersensitivity
Vedolizumab: Toxicity/overdose: Infections and rare liver injury; PML not reported to date but vigilance advised; gut-selective with less systemic immunosuppression
Vedolizumab: Formulation: IV 300 mg vial; SC pen 108 mg. Adult dose: 300 mg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks; SC 108 mg every 2 weeks after IV induction.
Vedolizumab: The IBD biologic that is most gut-selective.
Ustekinumab — Human anti-IL-12/23 antibody
Ustekinumab: Blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling.
Ustekinumab: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis
Ustekinumab: Nasopharyngitis, injection-site reactions, headache, fatigue
Ustekinumab: Hypersensitivity
Ustekinumab: Toxicity/overdose: Serious infections, TB, reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy (rare), hypersensitivity
Ustekinumab: Formulation: IV 130 mg/26 mL vial; SC 45/90 mg. Adult dose: IV induction by weight (260 mg under 55 kg, 390 mg 55-85 kg, 520 mg over 85 kg), then 90 mg SC every 8 weeks.
Cyanocobalamin — Vitamin
Cyanocobalamin: Replaces vitamin B12 (absorption needs stomach acid to free it from food and intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum).
Cyanocobalamin: B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, PPI or metformin-related deficiency
Cyanocobalamin: Injection-site pain, mild diarrhea, itching; early low potassium when treating severe anemia
Cyanocobalamin: Cobalt allergy, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
Cyanocobalamin: Toxicity/overdose: Low toxicity; excess is excreted; folate alone can mask B12 anemia while neuropathy progresses
Cyanocobalamin: Formulation: Tablet 100-1,000 mcg; IM injection 1,000 mcg/mL; nasal gel. Adult dose: Deficiency: 1,000 mcg IM daily for 1 week, then weekly, then monthly; or 1,000-2,000 mcg PO daily.
Cyanocobalamin: Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users; treat with IM or high-dose oral B12.
Folic acid — Water-soluble vitamin
Folic acid: Replaces folate (water-soluble vitamin B9).
Folic acid: Megaloblastic anemia, pregnancy, sulfasalazine and methotrexate therapy
Folic acid: Nausea, bloating, rash (rare)
Folic acid: Untreated B12 deficiency (can mask anemia)
Folic acid: Toxicity/overdose: Low toxicity; high doses may mask B12 deficiency and worsen neurologic injury
Folic acid: Formulation: Tablet 0.4/0.8/1 mg; injection. Adult dose: Deficiency 1 mg PO daily; 0.4 mg daily for neural tube defect prevention (4 mg if prior NTD).
Folic acid: Critical in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.
Vitamin D — Fat-soluble vitamin
Vitamin D: Fat-soluble vitamin; deficiency impairs bone mineralization.
Vitamin D: Rickets, osteomalacia, osteoporosis support, deficiency
Vitamin D: Usually none; nausea and constipation with excess
Vitamin D: Hypercalcemia, hypervitaminosis D
Vitamin D: Toxicity/overdose: Toxicity: hypercalcemia, kidney stones, calcification; fat-soluble so accumulates
Vitamin D: Formulation: Capsule/tablet 400-5,000 IU; 50,000 IU capsule. Adult dose: Maintenance 600-800 IU PO daily; deficiency 50,000 IU weekly for about 8 weeks.
Phytonadione — Fat-soluble vitamin
Phytonadione: Vitamin K1: supports carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, opposing warfarin.
Phytonadione: Warfarin reversal, vitamin K deficiency bleeding, malabsorption
Phytonadione: Injection-site reactions; flushing
Phytonadione: Hypersensitivity
Phytonadione: Toxicity/overdose: IV: boxed warning for anaphylaxis (infuse slowly); overcorrection causes warfarin resistance
Phytonadione: Formulation: Tablet 5 mg; injection 10 mg/mL. Adult dose: Warfarin over-anticoagulation: 1-10 mg PO or slow IV by INR; newborn prophylaxis 0.5-1 mg IM.
Phytonadione: Warfarin patients: keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.
Ferrous sulfate — Iron supplement
Ferrous sulfate: Replaces iron; absorption enhanced by vitamin C, impaired by antacids and PPIs.
Ferrous sulfate: Iron-deficiency anemia
Ferrous sulfate: Constipation, nausea, dark stools, abdominal pain
Ferrous sulfate: Hemochromatosis, hemosiderosis, hemolytic anemia
Ferrous sulfate: Toxicity/overdose: Acute iron overdose is a pediatric emergency: GI bleeding, shock, liver failure; chelate with deferoxamine
Ferrous sulfate: Formulation: Tablet 325 mg (65 mg elemental); liquid. Adult dose: 325 mg PO once daily or every other day, ideally with vitamin C.
Ginkgo biloba — Herbal supplement
Ginkgo biloba: Herbal supplement that raises bleeding risk with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.
Ginkgo biloba: Self-treated memory complaints (limited evidence)
Ginkgo biloba: Headache, GI upset, dizziness
Ginkgo biloba: Bleeding disorders; stop before surgery
Ginkgo biloba: Toxicity/overdose: Increased bleeding with warfarin, antiplatelets, NSAIDs; seizures with seed ingestion
Ginkgo biloba: Formulation: Capsule/tablet 40-120 mg. Adult dose: 120-240 mg/day PO in divided doses; not FDA-approved for treatment.
Ginkgo biloba: Ask about supplements at every medication reconciliation.
Fish oil — Dietary supplement
Fish oil: Omega-3 fatty acids; raise bleeding risk at high doses with anticoagulants.
Fish oil: Hypertriglyceridemia, cardiovascular risk reduction (Rx)
Fish oil: Fishy aftertaste, belching, diarrhea
Fish oil: Hypersensitivity; fish or shellfish allergy (caution)
Fish oil: Toxicity/overdose: Bleeding risk at high doses with anticoagulants; atrial fibrillation at high doses
Fish oil: Formulation: Capsule 300-1,000 mg EPA/DHA; Rx icosapent ethyl 1 g. Adult dose: 1-4 g/day EPA plus DHA PO; Rx forms for hypertriglyceridemia.
Furosemide — Loop diuretic
Furosemide: Loop diuretic: blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb (~25% of filtered Na⁺) and collapses the lumen-positive potential → ↑ Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ excretion.
Furosemide: Edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, kidney disease), hypertension, acute pulmonary edema, hypercalcemia
Furosemide: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, volume depletion, hyperuricemia, ototoxicity
Furosemide: Anuria, hypersensitivity; use caution with sulfonamide allergy (low cross-reactivity), hepatic coma
Furosemide: Toxicity/overdose: Ototoxicity with rapid IV or high doses, severe volume and electrolyte depletion, AKI; monitor potassium, magnesium, creatinine

Furosemide: Formulation: Tablets 20/40/80 mg; oral solution; IV injection 10 mg/mL. Adult dose: Edema: 20-80 mg PO once or BID, titrate to response (up to 600 mg/day in severe CKD or HF); IV 20-40 mg slowly (no faster than 4 mg/min).
Furosemide: Preferred over thiazides in edema and advanced CKD (GFR < 30); give IV no faster than 4 mg/min.
Furosemide: Hypokalemia raises digoxin toxicity; aminoglycosides add ototoxicity; NSAIDs blunt the effect.
Furosemide: Hypercalcemia: give with saline — a loop alone causes volume contraction.
Furosemide: Digoxin: loop hypokalemia increases toxicity. Aminoglycosides: additive ototoxicity. NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.
Bumetanide — Loop diuretic
Bumetanide: Loop diuretic: blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb; about 40× furosemide potency mg for mg.
Bumetanide: Edema in heart failure, hepatic and renal disease
Bumetanide: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, muscle cramps, dizziness, ototoxicity
Bumetanide: Anuria, hepatic coma, severe electrolyte depletion, hypersensitivity
Bumetanide: Toxicity/overdose: About 40 times more potent than furosemide mg for mg; profound diuresis, hypokalemia, ototoxicity
Bumetanide: Formulation: Tablets 0.5/1/2 mg; IV injection 0.25 mg/mL. Adult dose: Edema: 0.5-2 mg PO once or BID (maximum 10 mg/day); IV 0.5-1 mg.
Bumetanide: About 40 times more potent than furosemide mg for mg.
Bumetanide: Digoxin: loop hypokalemia increases toxicity. Aminoglycosides: additive ototoxicity. NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.
Torsemide — Loop diuretic
Torsemide: Loop diuretic: blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.
Torsemide: Edema in heart failure, kidney disease, cirrhosis; hypertension
Torsemide: Hypokalemia, dizziness, headache, hyperuricemia, ototoxicity (less than furosemide)
Torsemide: Anuria, hypersensitivity (sulfonylurea or sulfonamide allergy caution)
Torsemide: Toxicity/overdose: Volume depletion, hypokalemia, hypotension; longer half-life and more predictable absorption than furosemide
Torsemide: Formulation: Tablets 5/10/20/100 mg. Adult dose: Edema: 10-20 mg PO daily (up to 200 mg/day); hypertension: 5 mg daily.
Torsemide: Longer half-life and more predictable absorption than furosemide; less ototoxicity.
Torsemide: Digoxin: loop hypokalemia increases toxicity. Aminoglycosides: additive ototoxicity. NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.
Hydrochlorothiazide — Thiazide diuretic
Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide: blocks the Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule (~5–8% of Na⁺); lower cell Na⁺ drives NCX Ca²⁺ reabsorption → ↓ urinary Ca²⁺.
Hydrochlorothiazide: First-line hypertension, mild edema, calcium kidney stones, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Hydrochlorothiazide: Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia and gout, photosensitivity
Hydrochlorothiazide: Anuria, sulfonamide allergy; less effective when GFR is below about 30 mL/min
Hydrochlorothiazide: Toxicity/overdose: Severe hyponatremia and hypokalemia, volume depletion, hypercalcemia; monitor sodium, potassium, calcium, glucose
Hydrochlorothiazide: Formulation: Tablets 12.5/25/50 mg; capsules 12.5 mg; many fixed combinations. Adult dose: Hypertension: 12.5-25 mg PO daily (maximum 50 mg); edema: 25-100 mg daily.
Hydrochlorothiazide: First-line for essential hypertension with preserved renal function; loses efficacy below GFR ~30 — switch to a loop.
Hydrochlorothiazide: Hyponatremia in older adults; raises lithium levels; useful for calcium stones and osteoporosis.
Hydrochlorothiazide: Hyperglycemia mainly above 50 mg/d.
Hydrochlorothiazide: Lithium levels rise; NSAIDs blunt the effect.
Chlorthalidone — Thiazide-like diuretic
Chlorthalidone: Thiazide-like: blocks NCC in the distal convoluted tubule; same site as HCTZ, longer action.
Chlorthalidone: Hypertension (longer duration, often preferred), edema
Chlorthalidone: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia, erectile dysfunction
Chlorthalidone: Anuria, sulfonamide allergy, severe hypokalemia
Chlorthalidone: Toxicity/overdose: Profound hypokalemia and hyponatremia (more than hydrochlorothiazide at equal dose); long half-life of 40-60 hours
Chlorthalidone: Formulation: Tablets 12.5/25/50 mg. Adult dose: Hypertension: 12.5-25 mg PO daily (maximum 50 mg); edema: 50-100 mg daily.
Chlorthalidone: Often preferred for 24-hour BP control (half-life 40–60 h); more hypokalemia and hyponatremia than HCTZ at equal dose.
Chlorthalidone: Lithium levels rise; NSAIDs blunt the effect.
Spironolactone — Aldosterone receptor antagonist (potassium-sparing)
Spironolactone: Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor antagonist in the collecting duct → less ENaC and Na/K pump activity → less K⁺ and H⁺ secretion; also antiandrogen.
Spironolactone: Heart failure, resistant hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism, edema, ascites
Spironolactone: Hyperkalemia, gynecomastia, menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, GI upset
Spironolactone: Hyperkalemia, Addison disease, anuria; avoid with potassium supplements and caution with ACE inhibitors or ARBs
Spironolactone: Toxicity/overdose: Life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in CKD or with ACE inhibitor/ARB; monitor potassium and creatinine within 1 week
Spironolactone: Formulation: Tablets 25/50/100 mg; oral suspension. Adult dose: Hypertension: 25-100 mg daily; heart failure: 12.5-25 mg daily; primary hyperaldosteronism: 100-400 mg daily.
Spironolactone: Hyperkalemia, especially with ACE inhibitors/ARBs or CKD — check potassium and creatinine within 1 week; gynecomastia.
Spironolactone: Cirrhotic ascites responds well; RALES benefit in severe heart failure.
Spironolactone: Hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, trimethoprim, or CKD.
Eplerenone — Selective aldosterone receptor antagonist
Eplerenone: Selective aldosterone receptor antagonist in the collecting duct; far fewer antiandrogen effects than spironolactone.
Eplerenone: Heart failure after myocardial infarction, hypertension
Eplerenone: Hyperkalemia, dizziness, hypertriglyceridemia, fewer antiandrogen effects
Eplerenone: Potassium above 5.5 mEq/L, CrCl below 30 mL/min, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole)
Eplerenone: Toxicity/overdose: Hyperkalemia; levels rise sharply with CYP3A4 inhibitors; monitor potassium and creatinine
Eplerenone: Formulation: Tablets 25/50 mg. Adult dose: Heart failure post-MI: 25 mg daily, increase to 50 mg; hypertension: 50 mg daily, may increase to BID.
Eplerenone: Choose over spironolactone when gynecomastia is a problem; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, K⁺ > 5.5 or CrCl < 30.
Eplerenone: Hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, trimethoprim, or CKD.
Eplerenone: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole) raise levels sharply.
Amiloride — ENaC blocker (potassium-sparing)
Amiloride: ENaC blocker: blocks the collecting-duct sodium channel directly, independent of aldosterone → less K⁺ and H⁺ secretion.
Amiloride: Adjunct to loop or thiazide to preserve potassium, lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Amiloride: Hyperkalemia, nausea, headache, weakness
Amiloride: Potassium above 5.5 mEq/L, anuria, significant renal impairment, concomitant potassium supplements
Amiloride: Toxicity/overdose: Hyperkalemia with arrhythmias, especially in diabetes and CKD; monitor potassium
Amiloride: Formulation: Tablets 5 mg. Adult dose: 5 mg PO daily, may increase to 10 mg (maximum 20 mg/day).
Amiloride: Adjunct to a loop or thiazide to preserve potassium; lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Amiloride: Hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, trimethoprim, or CKD.
Triamterene — ENaC blocker (potassium-sparing)
Triamterene: ENaC blocker: blocks the collecting-duct sodium channel directly, independent of aldosterone.
Triamterene: Edema, hypertension, hypokalemia prevention
Triamterene: Hyperkalemia, nausea, kidney stones, blue urine, folate antagonism
Triamterene: Hyperkalemia, severe renal impairment, anuria, concomitant potassium supplements
Triamterene: Toxicity/overdose: Hyperkalemia, nephrolithiasis, AKI with NSAIDs; monitor potassium and creatinine

Triamterene: Formulation: Capsules 50/100 mg; combination tablets with hydrochlorothiazide (37.5/25 and 75/50 mg). Adult dose: Alone: 100 mg PO BID (maximum 300 mg/day); combination: 37.5/25 to 75/50 mg daily.
Triamterene: Combined with HCTZ (Maxzide, Dyazide); kidney stones, blue urine; AKI with NSAIDs.
Triamterene: Hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, trimethoprim, or CKD.
Triamterene: AKI with NSAIDs (indomethacin).
Acetazolamide — Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Acetazolamide: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: blocks Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ reabsorption in the proximal tubule → bicarbonate diuresis and metabolic acidosis; weak diuretic.
Acetazolamide: Glaucoma, altitude sickness prophylaxis, metabolic alkalosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Acetazolamide: Metabolic acidosis, paresthesias, hypokalemia, kidney stones, taste changes
Acetazolamide: Sulfonamide allergy, severe renal or hepatic disease, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, adrenal failure
Acetazolamide: Toxicity/overdose: Severe metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, confusion, bone marrow suppression (rare)

Acetazolamide: Formulation: Tablets 125/250 mg; extended-release capsules 500 mg; IV 500 mg. Adult dose: Glaucoma: 250 mg PO 1-4 times daily; altitude sickness: 125-250 mg BID starting a day before ascent; edema: 250-375 mg daily.
Acetazolamide: Niche uses: glaucoma, altitude sickness (start a day before ascent), metabolic alkalosis; sulfonamide caution.
Acetazolamide: Sulfonamide allergy: use caution.
Mannitol — Osmotic diuretic
Mannitol: Osmotic diuretic: filtered but poorly reabsorbed, so it holds water in the tubule lumen; draws water out of cells (lowers ICP/IOP).
Mannitol: Raised intracranial pressure, raised intraocular pressure, oliguria prevention in selected cases
Mannitol: Fluid and electrolyte shifts, headache, nausea, thirst, hyponatremia
Mannitol: Anuria, severe dehydration, active intracranial bleeding, severe pulmonary edema, heart failure
Mannitol: Toxicity/overdose: Volume overload with pulmonary edema, hyperosmolality, AKI, hypo- or hypernatremia; monitor osmolality and electrolytes
Mannitol: Formulation: IV solutions 10%, 15%, 20% and 25%. Adult dose: Raised ICP or IOP: 0.25-1 g/kg IV over 30-60 minutes; repeat 0.25-0.5 g/kg every 4-8 hours as needed.
Mannitol: Raised ICP/IOP; needs intact renal perfusion; avoid in heart failure and volume depletion; monitor osmolality and electrolytes.
Captopril — ACE inhibitor

Captopril: Blocks ACE (angiotensin I → II): less vasoconstriction and aldosterone; also less bradykinin breakdown (cough, angioedema). Dilates the efferent arteriole → ↓ intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
Captopril: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy
Captopril: Cough, hyperkalemia, hypotension, taste change, rash, angioedema
Captopril: Pregnancy, history of angioedema with ACE inhibitors, bilateral renal artery stenosis, concomitant aliskiren in diabetes
Captopril: Toxicity/overdose: Angioedema, hyperkalemia, hypotension, AKI; take 1 hour before meals; monitor potassium and creatinine
Captopril: Formulation: Tablets 12.5/25/50/100 mg. Adult dose: Hypertension: 12.5-25 mg PO BID-TID (maximum 450 mg/day); heart failure: 6.25-12.5 mg TID.
Captopril: First-line in proteinuric CKD; creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected — continue; more → renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
s: L10 S5; S8; S10; SG U5-R9

t: Captopril: Contraindicated in pregnancy; check potassium and creatinine within 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules (hold in vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration).
Captopril: Hyperkalemia with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim; triple whammy AKI with an NSAID plus a diuretic; never with aliskiren in diabetes.
Lisinopril — ACE inhibitor

Lisinopril: Blocks ACE (angiotensin I → II): less vasoconstriction and aldosterone; also less bradykinin breakdown (cough, angioedema). Dilates the efferent arteriole → ↓ intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
Lisinopril: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy
Lisinopril: Dry cough, dizziness, hyperkalemia, creatinine rise up to 30%, angioedema
Lisinopril: Pregnancy, angioedema history, bilateral renal artery stenosis, concomitant aliskiren in diabetes
Lisinopril: Toxicity/overdose: Angioedema, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, AKI during volume depletion
Lisinopril: Formulation: Tablets 2.5/5/10/20/30/40 mg. Adult dose: Hypertension: 10 mg PO daily, titrate to 40 mg (maximum 80 mg); heart failure: start 2.5-5 mg daily.
Lisinopril: First-line in proteinuric CKD; creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected — continue; more → renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
s: L10 S5; S8; S10; SG U5-R9

t: Lisinopril: Contraindicated in pregnancy; check potassium and creatinine within 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules (hold in vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration).
Lisinopril: Hyperkalemia with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim; triple whammy AKI with an NSAID plus a diuretic; never with aliskiren in diabetes.
Enalapril — ACE inhibitor (prodrug)

Enalapril: Blocks ACE (angiotensin I → II): less vasoconstriction and aldosterone; also less bradykinin breakdown (cough, angioedema). Dilates the efferent arteriole → ↓ intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
Enalapril: Hypertension, heart failure, asymptomatic LV dysfunction
Enalapril: Cough, hyperkalemia, dizziness, hypotension, angioedema
Enalapril: Pregnancy, angioedema history, bilateral renal artery stenosis
Enalapril: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, hyperkalemia, angioedema, AKI; reduce dose when CrCl is below 30 mL/min
Enalapril: Formulation: Tablets 2.5/5/10/20 mg; IV enalaprilat. Adult dose: Hypertension: 5 mg PO daily, titrate to 40 mg daily or divided; heart failure: 2.5 mg BID.
Enalapril: First-line in proteinuric CKD; creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected — continue; more → renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
s: L10 S5; S8; S10; SG U5-R9

t: Enalapril: Contraindicated in pregnancy; check potassium and creatinine within 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules (hold in vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration).
Enalapril: Hyperkalemia with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim; triple whammy AKI with an NSAID plus a diuretic; never with aliskiren in diabetes.
Losartan — Angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB)
Losartan: Blocks the AT1 receptor directly; no bradykinin rise, so no cough. Same efferent-arteriole renoprotection as ACE inhibitors.
Losartan: Hypertension, diabetic nephropathy, stroke risk reduction with LV hypertrophy, heart failure alternative
Losartan: Dizziness, hyperkalemia, creatinine rise, rare angioedema
Losartan: Pregnancy, concomitant aliskiren in diabetes, bilateral renal artery stenosis
Losartan: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, hyperkalemia, fetal toxicity; no bradykinin cough
Losartan: Formulation: Tablets 25/50/100 mg. Adult dose: Hypertension: 50 mg PO daily, up to 100 mg; diabetic nephropathy: 50 mg daily, increase to 100 mg.
Losartan: The usual switch for ACE-inhibitor cough.
Losartan: First-line in proteinuric CKD; creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected — continue; more → renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
s: L10 S5; S8; S10; SG U5-R9

t: Losartan: Contraindicated in pregnancy; check potassium and creatinine within 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules (hold in vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration).
Losartan: Hyperkalemia with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim; triple whammy AKI with an NSAID plus a diuretic; never with aliskiren in diabetes.
Valsartan — Angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB)
Valsartan: Blocks the AT1 receptor directly; no bradykinin rise, so no cough. Same efferent-arteriole renoprotection as ACE inhibitors.
Valsartan: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI
Valsartan: Dizziness, hyperkalemia, fatigue, creatinine rise
Valsartan: Pregnancy, concomitant aliskiren in diabetes, bilateral renal artery stenosis
Valsartan: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, hyperkalemia, fetal toxicity
Valsartan: Formulation: Tablets 40/80/160/320 mg. Adult dose: Hypertension: 80-160 mg PO daily (maximum 320 mg); heart failure: 40 mg BID, titrate to 160 mg BID.
Valsartan: The usual switch for ACE-inhibitor cough.
Valsartan: First-line in proteinuric CKD; creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected — continue; more → renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
s: L10 S5; S8; S10; SG U5-R9

t: Valsartan: Contraindicated in pregnancy; check potassium and creatinine within 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules (hold in vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration).
Valsartan: Hyperkalemia with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim; triple whammy AKI with an NSAID plus a diuretic; never with aliskiren in diabetes.
Aliskiren — Direct renin inhibitor
Aliskiren: Direct renin inhibitor: blocks the rate-limiting first step of the RAAS.
Aliskiren: Hypertension (rarely first-line)
Aliskiren: Diarrhea, cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema, hypotension
Aliskiren: Pregnancy; do not combine with ACE inhibitors or ARBs in diabetes or with eGFR below 60 mL/min
Aliskiren: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, hyperkalemia, AKI when combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs
Aliskiren: Formulation: Tablets 150/300 mg. Adult dose: 150 mg PO daily, may increase to 300 mg daily; take consistently with respect to meals.
Aliskiren: Limited use; not combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB (additive hyperkalemia and hypotension, no benefit).
Aliskiren: Never with ACE inhibitors or ARBs in diabetes or eGFR < 60.
Amlodipine — Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Amlodipine: Dihydropyridine CCB: arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload — the same mechanism treats hypertension and angina.
Amlodipine: Hypertension, chronic stable angina, vasospastic angina
Amlodipine: Peripheral edema, flushing, headache, dizziness, gingival hyperplasia
Amlodipine: Hypersensitivity, severe aortic stenosis (caution), cardiogenic shock
Amlodipine: Toxicity/overdose: Profound hypotension with reflex tachycardia, prolonged vasodilation; slow onset and long half-life
Amlodipine: Formulation: Tablets 2.5/5/10 mg; oral suspension. Adult dose: Hypertension or angina: 5 mg PO daily, up to 10 mg daily; start 2.5 mg in older or frail patients.
Amlodipine: Pairs safely with beta-blockers; peripheral edema is the class adverse effect.
Amlodipine: Grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.
Nifedipine ER — Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Nifedipine ER: Dihydropyridine CCB: arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload — the same mechanism treats hypertension and angina.
Nifedipine ER: Hypertension, chronic stable angina, vasospastic angina
Nifedipine ER: Peripheral edema, headache, flushing, reflex tachycardia, constipation
Nifedipine ER: Cardiogenic shock, hypersensitivity; avoid immediate-release forms in acute coronary syndrome
Nifedipine ER: Toxicity/overdose: Severe hypotension, reflex tachycardia, edema; swallow ER tablet whole
Nifedipine ER: Formulation: Extended-release tablets 30/60/90 mg. Adult dose: 30-60 mg PO daily, titrate to 90-120 mg daily; avoid immediate-release capsules for hypertension.
Nifedipine ER: Avoid immediate-release forms; peripheral edema, reflex tachycardia.
Nifedipine ER: Grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.
Diltiazem — Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Diltiazem: Non-dihydropyridine CCB: ↓ heart rate and contractility, ↑ coronary flow, plus arteriolar dilation.
Diltiazem: Hypertension, angina, atrial fibrillation rate control
Diltiazem: Bradycardia, AV block, edema, constipation, dizziness, CYP3A4 interactions
Diltiazem: Sick sinus syndrome, second- or third-degree AV block, severe hypotension, acute MI with pulmonary congestion, reduced EF
Diltiazem: Toxicity/overdose: Bradycardia, AV block, heart failure exacerbation; strongly interacts with beta-blockers

Diltiazem: Formulation: Tablets 30/60/90/120 mg; ER capsules 120-420 mg; IV injection. Adult dose: Hypertension: ER 120-240 mg PO daily up to 360 mg; angina: 30 mg QID (immediate-release) or ER daily.
Diltiazem: Avoid with beta-blockers (bradycardia, AV block).
Diltiazem: With a beta-blocker → bradycardia and AV block; raises digoxin levels; rifampin and carbamazepine lower levels.
Verapamil — Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Verapamil: Non-dihydropyridine CCB: ↓ heart rate and contractility, ↑ coronary flow, plus arteriolar dilation.
Verapamil: Hypertension, angina, atrial fibrillation and SVT rate control
Verapamil: Constipation, bradycardia, AV block, edema, dizziness, gingival hyperplasia
Verapamil: Sick sinus syndrome, AV block, severe LV dysfunction, WPW with atrial fibrillation, cardiogenic shock
Verapamil: Toxicity/overdose: Severe bradycardia, AV block, heart failure; avoid with beta-blockers; raises digoxin levels
Verapamil: Formulation: Tablets 40/80/120 mg; ER tablets 120/180/240 mg; IV injection. Adult dose: Hypertension: SR 180-240 mg PO daily up to 480 mg; angina: 80-120 mg TID.
Verapamil: Avoid with beta-blockers; constipation; raises digoxin.
Verapamil: With a beta-blocker → bradycardia and AV block; raises digoxin levels; rifampin and carbamazepine lower levels.
Atenolol — Beta-1 selective beta-blocker
Atenolol: Beta-1 selective blocker: ↓ heart rate, contractility and renin release.
Atenolol: Hypertension, angina, post-MI
Atenolol: Fatigue, bradycardia, cold extremities, depression, erectile dysfunction
Atenolol: Severe bradycardia, high-grade AV block, decompensated HF; do not stop abruptly
Atenolol: Toxicity/overdose: Accumulates in renal impairment, causing bradycardia and hypotension; rebound after abrupt withdrawal
Atenolol: Formulation: Tablets 25/50/100 mg. Adult dose: Hypertension: 25-50 mg PO daily (maximum 100 mg); reduce dose when CrCl is below 35 mL/min.
Atenolol: Accumulates in renal impairment — reduce dose when CrCl < 35 mL/min.
Atenolol: With diltiazem or verapamil → bradycardia, AV block.
Clonidine — Central alpha-2 agonist
Clonidine: Central α2 agonist: ↓ sympathetic outflow → ↓ BP.
Clonidine: Resistant hypertension, hypertensive urgency adjunct, opioid withdrawal adjunct
Clonidine: Sedation, dry mouth, bradycardia, constipation, rebound hypertension
Clonidine: Hypersensitivity; use caution in bradycardia and AV block
Clonidine: Toxicity/overdose: Rebound hypertension with abrupt withdrawal; overdose causes bradycardia, hypotension, coma and miosis
Clonidine: Formulation: Tablets 0.1/0.2/0.3 mg; transdermal patch 0.1-0.3 mg/day weekly. Adult dose: Hypertension: 0.1 mg PO BID, titrate (usual maximum 2.4 mg/day); patch 0.1 mg/day weekly.
Clonidine: Abrupt withdrawal → rebound hypertension; reserved for resistant hypertension.
Methyldopa — Central alpha-2 agonist
Methyldopa: Central α2 agonist: ↓ sympathetic outflow → ↓ BP.
Methyldopa: Hypertension in pregnancy, resistant hypertension
Methyldopa: Sedation, depression, dry mouth, positive Coombs test, hepatotoxicity
Methyldopa: Active liver disease, concomitant MAO inhibitors, history of methyldopa hepatitis
Methyldopa: Toxicity/overdose: Hemolytic anemia, hepatitis, drug fever; monitor liver tests and CBC
Methyldopa: Formulation: Tablets 250/500 mg. Adult dose: 250 mg PO BID-TID, titrate (maximum 3 g/day); preferred oral option for hypertension in pregnancy.
Methyldopa: Preferred oral option for hypertension in pregnancy.
Hydralazine — Direct arteriolar vasodilator
Hydralazine: Direct arteriolar vasodilator → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Hydralazine: Resistant hypertension, hypertensive emergency in pregnancy, heart failure (with nitrate)
Hydralazine: Headache, reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, flushing, drug-induced lupus
Hydralazine: Coronary artery disease without beta-blocker, mitral valve rheumatic disease, hypersensitivity
Hydralazine: Toxicity/overdose: Reflex tachycardia, angina, lupus-like syndrome with high dose or slow acetylators; pair with beta-blocker and diuretic

Hydralazine: Formulation: Tablets 10/25/50/100 mg; IV injection. Adult dose: Hypertension: 10 mg PO QID, titrate to 25-50 mg QID (maximum 300 mg/day); heart failure with isosorbide dinitrate: 25-75 mg TID.
Hydralazine: Must be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic; drug-induced lupus.
Isosorbide mononitrate — Organic nitrate (long-acting)
Isosorbide mononitrate: Releases nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venodilation → ↓ preload and O₂ demand.
Isosorbide mononitrate: Angina prophylaxis
Isosorbide mononitrate: Headache, dizziness, hypotension, flushing
Isosorbide mononitrate: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat, severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure
Isosorbide mononitrate: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, headache; tolerance requires nitrate-free interval

Isosorbide mononitrate: Formulation: ER tablets 30/60/120 mg; immediate-release tablets 10/20 mg. Adult dose: ER: 30-60 mg PO every morning, up to 240 mg/day; immediate-release: 20 mg BID given 7 hours apart.
Isosorbide mononitrate: Absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — life-threatening hypotension; nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.
Isosorbide mononitrate: PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat → severe hypotension.
Isosorbide dinitrate — Organic nitrate
Isosorbide dinitrate: Releases nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venodilation → ↓ preload and O₂ demand.
Isosorbide dinitrate: Angina prophylaxis, heart failure in Black patients (with hydralazine)
Isosorbide dinitrate: Headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia
Isosorbide dinitrate: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat, severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure
Isosorbide dinitrate: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, syncope, headache; tolerance without a nitrate-free interval

Isosorbide dinitrate: Formulation: Tablets 5/10/20/30/40 mg; ER capsules 40 mg; combination with hydralazine (BiDil). Adult dose: Angina: 10-40 mg PO TID with a 14-hour nitrate-free interval; heart failure: 20-40 mg TID with hydralazine.
Isosorbide dinitrate: Absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — life-threatening hypotension; nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.
Isosorbide dinitrate: With hydralazine for heart failure in Black patients.
Isosorbide dinitrate: PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat → severe hypotension.
